HEARTS may be honest, but they are always on the beat. WHAT sort of a room is best suited for poker playing? Why, an ante-room, of course. "1 SAY, Jim, if a fellow took sulphuric acid what would you give him?" "I'd give him up." A THING of beauty is a joy for ever, if you are wise enough to let some other fellow marry her. " YES, sir," said Popinjay, emphatically, "Graball is a man of limited means but unlimited meanness." THERE'S a man up town so cranky that he won't live in a house with trees in front of it, because, as be says, their bark disturbs him at night. A GERMAN baron is said to have secured a place as waiter in a New York restaurant. It is only natural that he should take to the fodderland. A TEMPERANCE lecturer in New Hampshire finished his discourse thus : "Finally, my hearers, why should any of you drink ardent spirits? My son Tom has got as good cider as any in the country, at six cents. per quart !" MR. Dnrooobs : "What a lovely colour Miss Jones has ! I declare, she looks like a chromo." Miss Smallwares : "A chromo ! I had the impres- sion that she was hand painted" NIAGARA LANDLOED : "You look tired and thirsty. Won't you have a glass of water?" Cautious Visitor (who has read about the Falls) : "How much is it?"
CHARLES LAMB said of the water-cure: "It is neither new nor wonderb,l, for it is as old as the Deluge, which, in my opinion, killed more than it cured." _ _

IT is an old adage that "Uneasy lies the head that wears a crown." It is equally true that un- easy lies the head that wears a presidential bee on its crown. "I WILL give you my heart, but not my hand," she whispered to him at the card table, and he didn't catch on until she showed four aces and took the pot. EIGHT mon outen ten is sorter 'dined ter be hippercrits, not so much 'case da wants ter be, but case da thinks dat eberybody else is an' dat mus' keep up wid de times." "PAPA, what does this mean : 'lt is better to give than to receive' ?'' asked a boy of his fond parent "It means, my son, that your mothe's finds more pleasure in lecturing me than I do in hearieg her." "The prettiest thing in bonnets," said Mrs. Bromley the other day, "is—" "Your face, Mrs. Bromley," said the old gentleman, gallantly; and Mrs. Bromley carried around a 9-inch smile for a week afterward. A lady said to her little daughter :—" This is your grandfather's birthday, Mamie. You must pray that he will live to an old age." Mamie— "No, ma, he is old enongh already. I'll just pray for hith to grow youueer instead of older.' There is a man in Berlin who has been a widower seven times. His seven wives have all died, but his seven mothers-in-law are in fine health, and are all living with him. There is Some talk of getting up a concert for his benefit." SOUTHEY once told Byron, who certainly did not agree with him, that "a man ought to be able to live with any woman '• " and this idea might probably be realised if the unfortunate husband would submit absolutely, even to the point of returning the wife in the Census (which happened more than once on the last occasion) as "head" of the family. "What is the most necessary thing in quench- ing a fire ?" asked a Texas teacher. " Water,' replied Johnny Fizzletop. "Not so, little boy. Fire is the most necessary, for if the fire didn't burn there would be no need of water. Savey ?" "See here, husband. The poet says Woman is the Sunday of man.' What do you think of that r "Pretty good for a poet. He's only one day off. If he had said either Monday—wash-day—or Saturday—pay-day—he'd been nearer right." A WOMAN always carries htr purse in her hand so that other women will see it ; a man carries his in his inside pocket so that his wife won't see it. A woman can sit in a theatre for three hours without getting all cramped up, catching the toothache, or becoming faint for want of fresh air; a man can't. A CYNICAL opponent of woman's suffrage insists that the invention of shirt studs is the Cause of woman's incursion into politics and other isms. He says that in the days of shirt buttons she had so much occupation in sewing them on that she could not give her attention to anything else. He sighs for the return of the good old times. GOOD GOVERNIIHNT.—A mad princess of the house of Bourbon, on beimg asked why the reigns of queens were, in general, snare prosperous than the reigns of kings, replied: " Because under kings women govera—under queens, meu." "HE called me an awl," exclaimed as over- dressed, excited dude. " Well, you ain't one," soothingly replied a kindly cop; "you are only a clothes horse." The body of a man who had drowned himself was taken from the water by a New York police- man. "Does anybody know anything about this man ?" asked the policeman of some urchins who were present. "We seed him just as ho came up for the last time, but we forgot ter ask him what his name was," said one of the boys. MRS. SMITHSON (who flatters herself upon her youthful appearance) : "That young lady over there is my daughter, Mr. Jones; would you believe it ?" Jones (looking in the wrong direc- ted) : "Your daughter! is it possible? I should have guessed she was your sister." Mrs. Smithson: "Not the lady you are looking at, Mr. Jones; she IS my mother." Jones "Oh !" CURIOUS NOTION OF DISCOUNT.—It chanced One gloomy day in the month of December that a good- humoured Irishman applied to a merchant to dis- count a bill of exchange for him at rather a long, though not an unusual date, and the merchant having casually remarked that the bill had a great many days to run "That's true," replied the Irishman, "but, then, my honey, you don't oon- Bider how short the days are at this time of the year." "Dor brudder of mine in Chicago vhas no good," said Moses, as he dusted a pair of second-hand trousers at the door ; "he close his shtore der odder day end puts on a sign dot his wife was dea.dt, mid he dean' keep open for two days." "Wasn't that right?" "It vhas all right to shut oop ; but why doan' he say on der sign, 'On die account I hal to dispose of dis mammoth shtock, nd all goods shall be sold at ten per cent, below coat? Viten a peeaness man's wife dies, it vhas a chance to advertise dot dean' come once in twenty years." SCHO'OLMASTER—"Noah had three sons, Shem, Ham and Japhet—now answer me: who was ot he father of these gentlemen?" (Boys silent.) "You cannot tell? Well, now let's try again. You know Mr. Sparkes, who lives over the way? Well, theta, Mr. Sparks has three boys—Tommy, John and Bill: now who was the father of these boys l" Boys—" Mister Sparkes " .31n4ler—" Very good. Now, then, Noah had three sons, Shem, Ham and Ja.phet : who—" Boys (in a hurry) —" Mr. Sparkes !" A HOUSEHOLD journal says that "a very pretty cover for a milking stool is made of golden-brown silk serge, with a conventionalised apple-blossom in shaded pink silk, with the stamens in gold silk betweeu the petals." Very gay, but a much prettier cover for a milking-stool ts a maid of golden-brown hair, rosy cheeks, silk-fringed eye- lids, and attired in a pink-muslin dress. But we don't often see them—outside of fiction. "What sort of a watc'3 is this?' asked Duzen- bury, picking up a curious old time-piece from an Austin watchmakers's show case. "That," replied the watchmaker, "is a real curiosity. It is a watch that belonged to Alexander the Great, when he died on the barren island of St. Helena." "The Sheol you say. Why, man alive, in the days of Alexander the Great they didn't have any watches." "That's j what makes it such rarity." "And Alexee. er the Great did not die at St. Helena." "He didn't eh ? Well, that makes it a still greater curiosity," and taking the rare relic from the hands of Durzenbury, he locked it up in his burglar proof safe. Miss Clara: "Can you call the name of the different stars and constellations, Mr. Featherly ?" Featherly : "Oh, yes. There is the north star and the evening star anti the Great Bear and the Milky Way, and all the rest. Oh, yes." Miss Clara: "The Great Bear is called Ursa Major, is it not ?" Featherly: "Oh, you mean do I know their botanical names? I m ashamed to confess I do not."

IF you set a vase of flowers in a current ot air they will lose their freshness in a very little time. They will also wilt quickly in a hot room. Always keep well sprinkled with cold water diming the day, and set them in the coolest part of the rooms and away from the open windows. In the night put them into the cellar and turn an air-tight vessel over them, after first covering them with a thin cloth well moistened. Often when they have begissto hang their heads during the day the treatment during the night revives them. Flowers preep longest in a temperature of from 40 deg. to 50 aboye Zero.

div.head: " CAPITAL " CHAT.
div.p: " CAPITAL " CHAT.

Mr. Schnadhorst, who left for Auatralia yester- day, had a meeting on Thursday with Mr. Glad- .tone, who wished him "Bon voyage." A number of political friends go with him to Liverpool-street Station or to the Albert Docks eer.erday to say good-bye," or, rather, " Au revoir."

Mrs. Annie Besant, who left Liverpool this week for New York, is not likely to be back in this country until the end of February. At all events her lecturing tour in America—including particu- larly the Pacific coast—is to be rather a long one. There is already in the States a fairly strong Theosophical society, but it is doubtful if it has among its members so silver-tongued a speaker as Mrs. Besant.

ir William Leece Driukwater, the first Deemster of the Isle of Man, who adjudicated in the Cooper case, is an old gentleman in his eighty-first year, who has been on the Manx judicial bench ever since 1847. Sir William, who is an M.A. of Cambridge, was called to the Bar at the Inner Ample in 1837. lie is a member of the Council, or Second Chamber, in the Isle of Man. salaries lf judges in the island are not extravagant; the pay of the First and Second Deernster is .Cl,OOO per annum.

The Rev. R. 11. Walker, the missionary who recently returned from Uganda, now that he has had a rest, is likely to address several meetings on the subject uf Uganda. Since he arrived in this coun- try he hes, with a Uganda chief, Sematimba, who accompanies him, been staying at his father's place near Yarmouth. Mr. Walker is perhaps a little over thirty, rather under the average height, and very sun-burned. He is a good speaker, and as he was in Uganda for several years he ought to have a good deal to say that is interesting about the country and the people.

Lord Rosebery, Mr. Arnold Morley, and Mr. Thomas Blackwell have each subscribed £lOO to the funds of the London Reform Union. Among other contributions are £5O from Mr. Passmore Edwards, £5O from Mr. John Barker, £2O from Sir Thomas Farrer, L.C.C., and £25 from Mr. IL L. Lawson. A general appeal is about to be issued. A lecture scheme, covering the whole ground of London municipal reform, is being prepared, and iti hoped ' that the whole series of seven lectures may be delivered in every constituency of London within four months.

Dr. Sedgwick Saunders, the City Medical Officer of Health, thinks that the magnitude of the epi- demic of scarlet fever amorg as will be better understood when the fact is realis.vd t rat no fewer than eleven hundred cases were reported in London the week before last. The bright spot in thia glcomy piece of statistics is that the attacks have all been of a mild type. This is shown by the fact that in the week referred to, out of 3,500 suffrirers only 27 died, whereas in the epidemic of 1870 the deaths were ()Ter 200 for several successive weeks, outof a population which at that time was only three-fourths that of the present day.

Professor Goldwin Smith, who is the latest of Mr. Gladstone's newspaper assailants,is a thin, medium- sized man, closely shaven, with very pale features, large dark eyes, and hair which is still dark, although lie is approaching his sixtieth year. His career at Oxford was phenomenal. He got the Hertford and Leland Scholarships, a First in Greats, and a host of university prizes, and found himself at five-and-thirty Regius Professor at Oxford of Modern History, a post which Mr. Froude was glad to accept in his seventy-sixth year. That chair Mr. Goldwin Smith resigned in 1868, and he has since lived in the United States and Canada, occasionally visiting England.

Mr. Goldwin Smith has a passion for attacking Premiers. Mr. Gladstone is not the first Prime Minister with whom the Professor has broken a lance. In his younger days Mr. Goldwin Smith, who was then a philosophic Radical, was fond of lecturing on Benjamin Disraeli. For a considerable period his assaults were unnoticed—once, indeed, Mr. Disraeli dubbed him contemptuously " that wild man." In " Lothair," however, which was published in 1870, after Mr. Goldwin Smith had emigrated to America, Disraeli sketched him as the "Oxford Professor." So well did the cap fit that Mr. Goldwin Smith wrote to the Tory leader from the other side of the Atlantic to say that he re- garded the attack as "the stingless insult of a cowaid."

Her Majesty has dons well in conferring all the honor there is in orders upon the handsome young Oaekwar of Baroda. No other Indian potentate— certainly no other representative of the Maratha races—hao show' such loyalty to the British Crown. Uniting the culture of the West with tho proverbial pertinacity and patience of tho typical Hindoo administrator, lie has very nicely balanced the conflicting interests of India and the British sovereignty ; and though intensely devoted to the faith of his ancestors, he has boldly and without hesitancy adopted as rapidly as these could be assimilated the doctrines and institutions of England. Sir Henry earkes, in his autobiography, men- tions that the richest man in Australia began his career on his savings as a farm labourer. The re- ference is to James Tyson, who is of Cumberland parentage, who is now worth some five millions sterling, and who, like Sir Henry himself, worked as a farm labourer in Australia for a wage of £3O per annum. It is curious that of these two men who began life as farm labourers, one should be- come a millionaire five times over, whilst the other should fail dismally in every business enterprise to which he turned his hand. Sir Henry, famous politician as he is, has never been able to make or keep money, and his chronic impecuniosity has long been a bye-word in the colonies.

Curiously enough, the biggest enterprise in which he embarked—the founding of a Sydney daily, the "Empire "—while it landed him in the Bonkruptcy Court, made the fortune of its printer, the late Samuel Bennett. This little shrewd, practical man bought the ruins of the " Empire" and on them erected what is now one cf the finest and most prosperous journalistic properties in the world—the Sydney" Evening News " and "Town and Country Journal." Mr. Ileaniker Heaton, now member for Canterbury and postal reformer of the universe, Owns a substantial interest in them.

There was a strong ,Calvinistic note about ,the speech of the Rev. J. A. Spurgeon at the annual meeting of the Pastors' Collage, on Thursday. He deplored the readiness of the church of the present day to" entertain " the people rather than to preach the Gospel,and said that the students of the Pastors' College at any rate were not trained to sing music- hall songs. The death of the Rev. Charles Spurgeon has been in no way detrimental to the prosperity of the College, there being no dearth of would-be students or want of work for those who have com- pleted their course. Professor Gracey, presith.nt of the College, gave an interesting account of the work done by past students, wlich he declared to be in many instances as heroic as anything in the history of evangelical religion.

A somewhat quaint story is told in connection with the peerage bestowed on a werthy supporter of the late Government on the eve of their retire- ment from office. It is customary for a commoner who is to be raised to the Upper House to select his new title, not out and out, as the general public are wont to suppose, but in a tentative manner by the suggeatton of two distinct titles, subject to the approval or disapproval of whatever may be the precise authority in such matters. The Conserva- tive M.P. to whom this story refers is stated to have sent in an ingenuous request fur the title of Lord Monmouth and Lord Southwark, and it was ap- parently much, to his astonishment that he was invited to supply a third alternative, on the ground that there were good and sufficient reasons against the two appellations on which he had so innocently set his heart.

"The Recollections of George Butler," recently compiled and published by his wife, Mrs. Josephine Butler, contains many anecdotes of the eminent people who were his friends. The Arnolds, Words- worth, and Hartley Coleridge were the intimates of his youth, and also Mr. J. A. Yroude, whom Canon Butler nursed through an attack of smallpox, after- wards taking the disease himself. After leaving the university he returned as public examiner alio lecturer on Art and Geography, which position he occupied till his wife's health compelled him to leave Oxford for Cliflon. Soon after he accepted the Principalship of Liverpool College, which he retained for sixteen years, until his appcintrr cut to the canonry of Winchester. During his active life he identified himself with the agitation promoted by Mrs. Butler for the repeal of c,rtain laws affect- ing her sex. Both lived to witnes s the triumph of their cause in 1886. Personally Canon Butler was a wan of fine presence and gentle manner, with a rare power of inspiring affection.

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 26, 1892.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 26, 1892.
PRIMITIVE METHODISM IN ItUNCORN.
LAYING FOUNDATION STONES OF A NEW SCHOOL.

For some years the Primitive Methodits of Runcorn have contemplated the erection of a school on the land adjacent to their chapel in Greenway- road, and when over twelve months ago the old building in Regent-street was disposed of to Mr Brunner. M.P., the project was one step nearer realisation. The second step was taken on Monday afternoon when the ceremony of laying the founda- tion stone was performed by Mr. J. F. L. Brunner, son of the esteemed M.P. for Northwich I dvision. The new school is to be tang of brick with stone and terracotta dressings, and is designed Mr. J. Wilson, the architect, to harnionise with the chapel, which adjoins. There are to be two front entrances into inner porches. The roof will be upon the hammer beaus prin- ciple. The interior arrangements are convenient and comfortable. There will be a large room capable of accommodating 400 persons, and on each side of this room will be two ordinary sized class-rooms and one , largo class-room, while there will also be three class- rooms across the end behind the platform, making a total of nine rooms. The large rooms are designed for the use of the adult classes, with a capacity for 40 scholars each ; and have glazed movable fronts, by which they can be added to the main room, thus increas- ing considerably the space necessary for lectures, enter- tainments, and other purposes. The superintendent's platform stands about 18 inches above the floor of the main room, having a circular front, and the superintend- ent will be in communication with every room by means of electric bells. The room immediately behind the plat- form is upon the same level, separated by revolving shutters, which will allow of it being used for the accommodation of a choir at concerts. The building will be lighted by coronas and side jets. The total estimated cost of the school is £1,350, including £2bo paid for the site. The contract for excavating, gra.nolithic, brickwork, plastering and slating his been I given to Messrs. Wilson and Sefton ; for mason work to I Mr. T. Robinson, and for joiners work to Mr. William I Bankes.

A large crowd of people assembled on the site for the purpose of watching the stonelaying ceremony. Amongst those noticed were the Revs. C. Finch, J. Watkin, (manager), and J. Simpson ; Messrs. J. F. L. Brunner, W. Shaw, W. Mundin, J. Spruce and F. Spruce (Preston Brook), Cowap (Preston Brook), Withinshaw (Dutton), J. Wilson, J. Sefton, S. Walton, .1. Whitley, D. Lewis (Widnes). W. Cooper (Widnes). ,kc. The proceedings commenced with the hymn " Blest is the man whose heart expands," and then the Rev. J. Watkin offered up prayer. The Bev. C. Pinch then presented Mr. Brunner with a silver trowel, with which to lay the foundation stone, in a cavity of which were placed a plan of the circuit copies of the local newspapers, and a few coins of the rea I m.

Mr. Brunner before proceeding to discharge his import- ant duty, congratulated those connected with the pro- ject for the very praiseworthy efforts they had made to have a suitable Sunday school. He understood they started somewhat in debt, but he hoped endeavours would be made to clear off the deficiency in a short time. It afforded him great pleasure to come to Runcorn to assist in adding another institution to the educational establishments of the town. He hoped the day was not far distant when all creeds and classes would go together for their education which was not religious, and then withdraw to an institution such as the one they were building for their religious education. He could not see why they should not have such an arrangement so that there would be so quarrelling as to what religious de- nomination should be managers of the day schools. In conclusion he thanked them for the very handsome trowel presented to him, and proceeded to lay the stone.

Memorial stones were also laid by Mrs. S. Walton, Mr. D. Lewis, Runcorn • Mrs. Collier (on behalf of the Ladies sewing meeting), 'Mrs. R. Abel, and Mr. F. Spruce (on behalf of Miss Salt of Preston Brook.) Each lady arid gentleman was presented with a handsome silver trewel. Mr. Lewis said he was pleased to be able to do something to show his indebtedness to a school in which be was once a scholar, and also in memory of his father and grandfather, who had been ardent workers in con- nection with the place. Appropriate remarks were also made by the other stonelayers. The last stone was laid by Mrs. Stubbs, who had been connected with the school about fifty years. Each child who had collected for the fund now came forward and laid a brick of the new building, as did a number of other persons present. On the proposition of the Rev. J. Watkin, seconded by the Rev. C. Finch a vote of thanks was heartily accorded to the ladiea and gentlemen who had assisted in the csremony, and the singing of the Doxology brought the proceedings to a conclusion. Subsequently tea was provided in Camden Wesleyan schoolroom, and in the evening a public meeting was held in Oreenway-road Chapel. There was a large attendance. Mr. P. Speakman presided, and on the platform were the Revs. J. Watkin (Manchester), T. Wilks (Wesleyan), R. D. Didcock (Frodshain), J. Simp- son (Congregational), J. Martin (Free Church), C. Pinch (the pastor). Messrs. F. L. Brunner, J. L. Spruce, D. Lewis, and John Wilson. The Rev. C. Finch made a statement of the finances. The land upon which they were about to erect schools la.ad cost them in round figures £250. They estimated that the building would cost about £1,200, making a total outlay of £1,450. They disposed of the old school in Regent-street to Mr. Brunner, who paid them the sum they asked, £4OO. (Hear, hear.) The late Mr. Samuel White left them £lOO, and the trustees had given them that sum towards the building fund of the school. Those connected with the chapel had promised amongst them £l5O, and he had reason to believe that the gift would exceed that amount. (Hear, hear.) That day at the stone-laying ceremony, Mrs. Walton gave a dona- tion of £2O, Mrs. Abel gave £5, Miss Salt £5, and Mr. Lewis £l5. (Applause.) The ladies' sewing meeting placed upon the stone, which Mrs. Collier laid on their behalf, the very handsome sum of 225. The Sunday School scholars and teachers had raised the sum of £45 7s. (Applause.) There was collected that day £6 183. 10d., and the laying of bricks brought in £2 165., and Mr. Whitley. one of the Wesleyan preachers frem Warrington, had handed . him balf-a.sovereign towards the building fund. He had also had promised £35, and he was pleased to say that sum included ten guineas promised by the Chairman, a similar sum by Mr. J. Simpson, and the remainder by Messrs. Wm. Hayes, J. Pritchard, F. and A. R. Norman. Those figures added made a total of £Bl3, which he thought was a good start—(hear, hear)—and he thought by the time tire building was up, and the opening service was over, they would have realized the handsome sum of £l,OOO. (Applause.) he Chairman, who had a cordial reception, said it was a great pleasure to be there that night. He liked to rejoice with those that rejoiced, and he was sure the ! ' Primitive Methodists of Runcorn, could not help but be full of joy at the laying of the foundation stone of the new schools, which had been talked about fir a number of years. He was pleased that their young .friend Mr. Brunner had been with them that day, and glad to think that he was a chip off the old block. (Applause.) They had evidences from day to day, that what Mr. Brunner, their member could do for them, he was always willing to do and he did it. (Applause.) Alluding to the work ' and influence of Sunday Schools, the chairman said he was now connected and always had been connected with Sunday school work, it was one of the pleasures of his life, and he urged those who did not take an active ,1 part in the work, to do so and they would find much personal benefit to result from it, while they were at the same time training the young to live a life of good- ness and purity. (Applause.) He wished them success' in obtaining the sum of money they required. (Applause.) . .

The Rev. T. Wilkes, expressed his sympathy with his Primitive Methodist friends, and remarking that Sunday Schools were modern institutions, and lie gave a short history of one established in 1785 :it Hulme. Sunday scbcols were the child of Methodism, and Methodists were glad that other churches bad adopted them and hoped they would keep them, and that God wculd make them a great blessing to th 3 churches. He referred to the time when reading and writing were taught in their Sunday schools, but they had now got board schools—and they had got denominational schools, but how long they would keep them he din not know nor did he care—and the teaching of such subjects was not necessary in their Sunday school of the present day, and he gave teachers some advice as to how to teach their scholars of Christ's great love, and bow to make the Sunday school a real training ground for the Church. The Rev. J. Watkin, in the course of an eloquent and impassioned address, said if a man who clearly saw what was the actual and the present, were asked what was the social condition of the country, he would tell of the national gambling, which like a fire was eating the very fibre and substance of the best and strongest man- hood of the country ; of the foul sin of impurity which lifted its brow in every place of public resort, and ex- haled its putrid breath from the periodical literature of the country, of drunkenness, that horrible vice of our nation, whose shadow dimmed the splendofir of our courts and palaces, and ascentuated the misety and poverty, and wretchedness of our slums. There was one class who were gifted with a higher and clearer and a spiritual vision, and who could not only see the actual and the present, but what was possible for the future. They said that Society was thus honey,oombed and weakened by these horrible vices. It was perhaps true that we bade fair to be the most drunken nation( upon the face of the earth, but 'God had created this great insti- tution of Sunday School teaching, and there were yet grander and brighter days before this, if they could sally make the influence of the Sunday School successful in the young life of. the nation. (Applause.) From a material point of view virtue paid. If we could rid Cho nation of these vicious and depraved habits, the nation would be saved 310 million pounds annually, and the great business of the Sunday Schools was to send out into the world healthy, honest, industrious, and thrifty citizens, and they could with confidence, ask for the sympathy and monetary help of Christian philantlfrop- ista on that account. (Applause.) The Rev. J. Simpson said he was very glad as a Con- gregationalist to stand upon the platform and wish them God speed. They were all Christians. Whatever might

be their creed or whatever church they belonged to, in the spirit of Christ they could all unite in Christian work. (Hear, hear.) The Rev. C. Finch moved a vote of thanks to the speaker, to the choir, to the workers.. that day, and to the trustees of the Camden School, for the use of their school.—Mr. D. Davies seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously. Mr. Brunner proposed a vote of thanks to the chair- man. He met Mr. Speakman on the committees of the County Council at Crewe and at the meetings of the Council at Chester, and he could assure them that in all the work there, Mr. Speaktnan's heart was in the right place ; and he knew that the work Mr. Speakman did in Runcorn was very valuable to the people. (Applause.) —Mr. John Wilson seconded the motion in complimen- tary terms, saying that Mr. Speakman was a representa- tive on the various public bodies, of whom they had reason to be proud.—The motion was carried by acclama- tion, and in reply the Chairman thanked the audience for their kind appreciation, and said they were welcome to his services. The collection realised £lO.

The silver trowel used by Mrs. Walton in laying the memorial stone was presented by Mr. W. Gittens. Mr. D. Lewis received his trowel at the hands of Mr. James Stubbs, Mrs. Abel at the hands of Mr. Aston, and the representative of Miss Salt at the hands of Mr. J. Fleet. The mallet used by Mrs. Stubbs was made and pre- sented by Mr. James Stubbs.
DISTURBANCE BY SHIP CANAL MEN AT WESTON POINT.

I Before Mr. Jas. Reynolds and Mr. A. Thomas, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Thomas Brown, Joseph Clough, Samuel Caldwell, Arthur Fletcher, and Richard Judkin, engine cleaneis on the Ship Canal, all of Frodsham, were charged with being drunk and refusing to quit the Dock Hotel, Weston Point, kept by William Grounds, at eleven o'clock on Saturday morning; and also with assault- ing P.C. Hammersley, at the same time and place, whilst in the execution of his duty—Thomas Grounds, brother of the landlord, stated at 10-45 the aocused came to his house. Four of them came in apparently sober, and they were served with half a gallon of beer. Soon afterwards he heard singing and dancing in the room, and on going there he &mud three others who were drunk. Thereupon he took the jug from them and asked them to leave, but they refused. They slammed the doors,threatened him,and stormed the bar. He was obliged te call in the services of the police. P.C. Hammerslev castle, and eventually, after a struggle,they got them outside. They then abused the constable in a scandalous manner. In answer to Clough, witness said he was one of the most sober to enter the house. Caldwell lie believed was one of the four who was served with beer.—George Myers, grocer, Weston Point,spoke to ,the assault upon the officer, and to his being ill-treated in a shameful manner. He did not know what the consequences might have been if help had not been given to the officer.—P.C. Hammersley stated that he was called in to the Dock Hotel on Saturday morning. He commenced to put the men out, and during the scuffle Brown hit him on the face. On reaching the strert they created a disturbance, and he tried to apprehend Brown twice but each time be got down, and before he could handcuff him the others rushed upon him. Whilst on the floor he felt two or three blows. He telephoned to .Runcorn for assist- ance.—lnspector Cooper deposed to chasing the men across Frodsham Marsh, having to get overohedges and ditches, the men being determined to escape.—Clough and Caldwell called the witness Grounds, who stated that the former was sober, and that the latter, in his opinion, was one of the first four to enter the house.— The Bench said they were of opinion that Brown, IFletcher, and Judkin were guilty of being drunk and refusing to quit the licensed premises, and they would be fined 103. and 93. 31 costs, or in default 14 days' imprisonment. Clough and Caldwell were not guilty. As to the assault on the constable, which was a most serious offence, they thought all five were equally guilty. They would each be fined £1 and Losts, or in default 14 days in gaol.

div.head: OSTRICH DANCING.
div.p: OSTRICH DANCING.

A writer of an interesting article on" Ostrich Dancing "in the " Californian IA agaline "for Octo- ber, mentions the following curious habit of the birds, a habit which is very expensive to their owners : _

Their peculiar habit of waltzing is worthy of note. It is usually done in the morning, when the sun comes up brightly, and they dance like a Der- vish, round and round, at such a rate that some- times it ends in a broken leg. Whether this is due to a twist the leg gets in crossing, or a sad ten iency of the bird to become giddy and tumble, with the above result, is a matter of opinion. Nevertheless it is said that in Africa, waltzing costs the owners eight to ten per cent, per annum, for if an ostrich breaks its leg it is almost certain not to recover. If any casualties have occurred among the Califor- nian birds on that account, they have not been reported. .
At Santa Monica an effort has been made to ride them, but there seemed to be no possibility of guid- ing them, and the project was abandoned.

div.head: HOW ATTAR OF ROSES IS MADE.
div.p: HOW ATTAR OF ROSES IS MADE.
' There is an interesting article in " Blackwood's Magazine" describing a visit to the great rose garden of the world in Bulgaria. The writer thus describes the manufacture of attar of roses :

In front of a long shed six large caldrons stood over the brazier, and into these vessels about a hundred pounds' worth of roses were put with warm water. The iron tubes through which the vapour escapes passed through a long tin receptacle shaped like a trough, which was filled with cold water, and below which large glass bottles stood to receive the first distillation. Three distillations are necessary before the oil of the rose appears. We were shown a small bottle into which the essense just distilled has been poured. The colour is a rich deep gold, and the smell is strong, substle and penetrating, pleasant for the first instant, but soon producing a sense of giddiness and oppression in the head. It affects everything near it, and the perfume clings tenaciously even in the open air. The proprietors are secured from being cheated, as the peasants cannot endure the perfume they them- selves manufacture, and make no use of it what- ever. It is sealed up in leaden bottles and sent to the great perfume emporiums in London and .Paris, and a thousand different scents each as have their essence a few drops of this rich thick oil. The bottles were large and flat, the shape of an ordinary hunting-flask, and sealed. He said that he sold the smaller ones at £2OO, £3OO, and MOO,
while he valued one large one at £l,OOO. When kept perfectly free of air, the essence is said to last un- impaired so long as 80 years.

div.head: STEEPLE-CHASING IN AUSTRALIA.
div.p: STEEPLE-CHASING IN AUSTRALIA.

Steeple-chasing is not the safest of amusements even in the old country, but judging from Mr. Dickinson's paper on " Racing in Australia " in Scribner it is child's play here compared with the way in which it is pursued in the Antipodes. Mr. Dickinson says:— Steeple-chasing, which is another popular feature of every meeting, is conducted upon a track just inside the main course, although at the finish the horsea cross outeide and end the race in the " straight" before the Grand Stand. This branch of the sport, as conducted on tie Flemington truck, is sufficiently exciting and dangerous. There is first presented to the horses a five-rail fence; then, in succession, a rail and paling fence each four feet three inches high ; a stone wAll capped with solid timber of four feet three and a half inches ; a log jump of three feet eleven inches; another post and rail of four feet ; a double-over post and rails of four feet and three inches ; and, following in order. four feet four inches of masonry and five more rail fences each four feet one inch in height. The fences are of the strongest possible construction, heavily bound and braced with iron, and absolutely rigid and immovable. In the great steeple-chase of the year—the " Grand National "—all these jumps have to be negotiated twice, the distance run being about three and one fifth miles. Few steeple- chases see more than half the horses engaged corn- in at the finish, but serious accidents are rare. The worst casuality in the Australian racing field occurr- ed on the Caulfield Course near Melborne. in 1885. when Too-Too, falling in the front rank of the field of forty-one horses, tripped up fifteen others that were following, and piled up racers and jockeys in a struggling mass. One man was killed, and five others were terribly injured, but finally recovered.

div.head: NO FREE EDUCATION'!
div.p: NO FREE EDUCATION'!
MR. ACLAND WARNS SCHOOL MANAGERS.

The following circular has been issued by the mana- gers of the Hyde British School : 1 Dear Sir,—Your child has comae to school without th, fees which are necessary. There is no such thing as free education. The new Act of Parliament only pro- vides for paying part of the fees in this school. If, how- ever, you appeal to our managers, and prove to them that poor circumstances make the payment of fees a hard- ship, they:will no doubt remit the other half of the fees, but until you have done this the fees must be paid. Mr. Ac!and has addressed the following letter to Mr. Thomas Proctor, of Gee-cross, Hyde, who wrote to him complaining that he sad other parents ia the district were unable to obtain free school places for their chil- dren without going through an 'ordeal of pauperism,' and that they still had to pay fees, in spite of having made representations to the Department :
'Education Dimartmeni, November 18th, 1892.

Dear Sir,—The Department are taking action to se- cure the provision ot the free school places claimed by you and other parents. But the means of doing se pro- vided by the Act of 1891 necessarily involve some delay where the demand for free places is not met by whin- tary local action. I have read with surprise and regret .the printed circular issued from Hyde British School and bearing upon it the names of the managers. It is an astonishing thing that such a circular,issued on the 11th of last month, should contain these words : There is no such thing as free education,' and should add that upon proof of poor circumstances,' a remission of fees will no doubt be obtained. It cannot be too clearly and widely understood that under the Act any and every parent in England and Wales irrespective of any question as to his means, is entitled to claim completely free education •for his children, and that it is the statutory duty of the Department to see that free education is provided accor- dingly. I would further express the hope that local school authorities, whether school beards or voluntary managers, will co-operate loyally in carrying out the intentions of Parliament, and will not make any ill- advised attempt to use the Act so as to raise distinctions of wealth and class or to attach invidious conditions to the acceptance of its benefits. Such action, if taken on any considerable scale, must inevitably result in fresh legislation, with the concurrence of both political parties, making such a publication as the circular you enclose an imposibility.—Yours faithfully, A. H. D. ACLAND.

div.head: RELIGIOUS EDUCATION. THE DEAN OF' MANCIIESTER WARR NGTON.I
div.p: RELIGIOUS EDUCATION. THE DEAN OF' MANCIIESTER WARR NGTON.I

A small public meeting in support of the National Society for the promotion of Religious Education was held in Cairo-st., Co-operative Hall, on Monday night. Mr. John White presided, and amongst those present were the Very Dean of Man- chester, Sir F. S. Powell, Bart., M.P., the Rev. F. G. Chandler (organising secretary), the Rev. Canon Penrhvn, the Rey. Morley Stevenson r(Principal of the Warrington Training College), Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, Rev. J. G. Langliain, and the Rev. H. V. Pigot. Letters of apology were received from Mr. Rote-rt Pierpoint, M,P., Mr. J. Charlton Parr, Dr. White, Rev. T. W. Cook, Rev. F. W. Willis, and Mr. ..Charles Marson.

The CHAinniete, in alluding to the small attendance, said that he had no doubt that this had been caused by the prevalence of the epidemic ; and he felt that he could not disagree with people in refusing to mix toge- ther at such a cri:ical time. In the course of his re- marks, he said lie had received a letter from a certain layman who said he could not be present, because he could not aeree to support the opening of another new society in Warrington. Well, all he had to say to that was, that the society, in the first place, was not a new one, for it had been in existence for the last 25 years. I And during that time it had done a considerable amount of beneficial work for Warrington, in achieving which it had expended at different times no less than £4,000, most of which had been devoted to providing school accommodation and religious education. Then, lie had received another letter from a gentleman who refused to attend because the society was promoting Church schools, whilst it was eviJent that nothing but Beard schools would soon exist. Well,, granting even that that was to a certain extent true, there would still remain for their society a great deal of work to be done for the training colleges. (Applause.) ' The Very Rev. the Dean of MANCHESTER, next spoke, and alluded to the amount of support given by the different dioceses of Manchester and Liverpool to the Society. He said the diocese of Manchester remitted to the society only £5OO a year, whilst that of Liverpool, with all its untold wealth, contributed the magnificent sum of £255 15s. 4d. Out of the £5OO contributed by I Manchester the cathedral deanery was foremost with Lug 15s. 9d. to its credit. (Applause.) With respect to the work of the society at the present critical time he could oily speak with bated breath. He was afraid of I what was paesiag in his own 'mind, but he thought that I those who were taking a deep interest in the education of the country should not be too pre- eipitate in expressing their opinionsv or form- ing hasty judgments. It had been urged that I soon the whole country would be covered with the school board system. He intended on that point merely to refer to the agricultural parts of the country, aid he would not embrace in his observations the I Principality of Wale, which they should always take as an integral part of the Church of England. However, in the agricultural districts we did not see any immedi- ate danger of the school board system being introduced, , or becoming prevalent. If the clergy and managers of I schools were wise in their generation he did not think that education was likely to be snatched out of their hands ; but on the contrary, those who viewed the posi- tion calmly and dispassionately would be likely to feel that after all School Attendance Committees and bodies of that kind would be more likely to put the hands of the educational dial backwards, rather than in the other direction. And consequently, in the rural dis- tricts, he contended there would still depend much upon the helpful agency of their national society. There seemed to be approaching a time when there would be what their opponents chose to term a national system of I education. That was what was brought within the range of those who professed practical politics. He lisped then that that education would continue to be what it had been in the past—an education based upon the principles of religion. (Applause.) This was so fully before the minds of the candidates who came forward at the last School Board elections in Salford and Manchester, that they were compelled to put forward in their pro- grammes "the maintenance of religious education." As Chairman of the Manchester School Board which had made such distinct progress, he could never honestly be a party to the habitation of schools, indiffer- ently equipped, iusanitarily appointed, and offer- ing an inferior education. As a member of the Church of Englaud he would not allow himself to be . dragged through such a slough of indifference and dis- : regard for the education of the country. (Applause.) He thought that the society was therefore doing well in ' directing itself to the class of work which it was at present carrying on, namely helping poor schools by itsi funds. He could see that the signs of the times were exceedingly portentous as regards the schools of the Church of England. In the city of Liverpool there was at the present time a great clamour for " free places" in schools, which would soon bring about a climax upon which he did not wish to dwell. He only hoped that what was dene by his colleagues on the Board lin Manchester would be done dispassionately, ' calmly and with due respect for the opinions of others. Especially did he commend to them the excellent purposes of the training colleges—one of which they poesessed in Warrington—and the character of the work which the students were capable of discharging after their studies. It was greatly to the students of .those colleges that they had to look for the teaching of religion in their schools. They got from those schools teachers who taught religiously all they taught, and not who merely taught religion, and he contended that was what was required. (Applause.) - .

Sir F. SHARP POWELL, M.P., who was received with applause, said that the income of the society was about £22,000. Up to two years ago the Church of Eugland had spent £30,250,000 in the building of schools, and £21,500,000 in the maintenance of schools, and upon training colleges they had spent £777,000. Between 1870 and 1891, extra accommodation was found in their schools for 1,305,000 children, and the average atten- dance had increased by 832,000. Their voluntary con- tribution from their own resources to Church schools had also increased from £589,640 in 1590 to £602,573 in 1891. (Bear, hear.) These were indications that their toil and bounty still continued. The meeting terminated with the usual vote of thanks.

div.head: lONIE,
div.p: lONIE,
PRIDE OF THE MILL
A THRILLING LOVE STORY. BY LAURA JEAN LIEBEY.
CHAPTER XXXII. lONIE'S PITIFUL SACRIFICE.

Mrs. Malcolm's warning 'yid come too late. Her son's heart had gone out to lonic with a passionate love that often frightened even himself by its in- tensity. He began to look forward with dread to the hour when she would leave them. It was at the end of the fourth week that she woke to the realisation of events transpiring about her.

After a deep sleep, her eyes had opened with the first faint gleam of consciousness in them, rest- ing upon the honest, toilworn faced grouped about the room and her unfamiliar surroundings. "Am I dreaming?" she murmured, struggling up to a sitting posture and gazing in bewilderment about her.

Mrs. Malcolm was by her side in an instant. "Of course you don't know where you are, dearie," she said. "This is a strange place to you." "My husband and my son found you struggling in the water and brought you here, where you have been lying so ill we thought you would die from day to day for the last four weeks. When you get better you will tell us who you are, and how you came to be in the water."
lonie had sunk back on her pillow with a shudder- ing cry. " Oh, I remember all now; I fell from the yacht. No one heard my cry as I was falling, and after I touched the water I knew no more.

"I have been here four weeks, you say?" she asked, incredulously. "Oh, Heaven, how terrified my dear uncle must have been, for he must believe me drowned. I pray you, my good woman, tele- graph to him at once, and he will pay you hand- somely for the great service you have rendered me. Or stay; so little can be said in a telegram; a letter explaining all to him would be best."

Propped up with pillows, a pen and parer was brought her, and lonie wrote the letter which was to bring about so much woe, little dreaming that her uncle, Colonel Whitney, lay, at that moment, in his grave. It was sealed, directed and stamped, and honest Will Malcolm took it himself to the letter-box.

No one can tell whether it is a fate that governs these things, or an evil star; but it so happened, on the day lonie's letter reached New York, and it was given into the postman's hands that served that fashionable thoroughfare in which the colonel had resided, that Frank Lyons, moody and angry at fate, was sauntering up Lexington Avenue. For a moment he stood gazing up at the closed windows of the mansion with darkening brows. "But for that girl's flight, all this would be mine now," he muttered. "I beg your pardon, sir," said a voice close beside him; "I remember you as a friend of he family. See this, sir—a letter for the poor coloneL Evidently the writer has not heard of his death." _

One glance at the delicate chirography on the envelope, and Frank Lyons could scarcely express the exultant cry that rose to his lips. He had recognised the handwriting of lonia. He must possess that letter at any cost, he told himself; and on the spur of the moment a daring idea occurred to him. He turned to the man with a well simulated cry of surprise. "Why. I declare, this is ray letter to the colonel," he said. "You are right. I did not know of his death until I reached here. This has been delayed. It ought to have preceded me by a day at least. I will take it, please."
Never suspecting a gigantic fraud, the postman bowed and moved on, and never thought of the incident again until it was brought back to his memory by a startling circumstance some time after.

Thrusting the letter carelessly into his pocket, Lyons sauntered on, to allay the postman's sus- picions; this is, if he entertained any. He could scarcely restrain his impatience, how- ever, to learn its contents.

Signalling a passing coupe, he entered it, giving the order to his hotel, and before he had traversed half the way to his destination he knew all. His exultation to learn her whereabouts, and that she had not fled from him, as he had supposed, but had been detained by a- most d itiaAIINIS accident instead, can better be imagined than deseribed. He was a rapid thinker, qui.* to plot and coun- terplot, mad as he leaned beak in the earriage a mast bold aud daring scheme oiteesesol to him. "I shall go on at oncei" ha nattered, an evil smile playing about his lips. "And she shall not know of the colonel's death until after I have made her my bride. If she knew of that she would defy me; my power over her would be at an end." It was late on the afternoon of the following day that Frank Lyons presented himself at the humble borne of the Malcolms.
louie was sitting up for the fist time that day, arrayed in the pretty white mull dress she had worn to that eventful yachting party, and which had been freshly laundried by Mrs. Malcolm.
"The gentleman you have 'been expecting all day has come at last, Miss." said Mrs. Malcolm, thrust- ing her ruddy face in at the sitting-room door. " Shall I snow him in here?"
" It. is uncle!" cried lonie, joyfully, "Yes, show him in here."

With joyful anticipation she watched the door, but the smile died from her lips and the light from eyes when, a moment later, she beheld standing on the t hrethold—lfrank Lyons 1 • , She sank back in her chair With a gasp of bitter disappointment. He came eagerly forward. "bole, my chiding !" he cried, rapturously. "My uncle is not with you?" she asked, interro- gatively, glancing past him towards the door. "1 am come in his stead, lonie," he answered. "Your letter was placed in my hands, and when I read it I lost no time in reaching here. No words can tell you my delight at seeing you; for we had given you up as lost. You will never realise the anritty, the sorrow you have caused us."

lam truly sorry," answered lonie. "I am very weak yet," he continued; "still I am anxious to reach home at the earliest possible moment." " Your words touch upon a subject uppermost in my heart," he said, drawing his chair nearer to her and flushing slightly. "Your uncle has given me a message for you, lonie," he said, boldly, "and he trusts you will see the wisdom of obeying his wishes in the matter, and that is—that I will bring you back with me— my wife."_

• A cry of dismay broke from the girl's lips, but he never heeded it; he went on, hurriedly: "He insists, nay, commands, that it shall be so; desiring me to add, that this hitherto unaccount- able absence has created no end ot scandal, so much so that he would feel it a strict duty to close his doors against you, unless, as I repeat, you return— my wife." lonie, weak as she was, sprang to her feet, white with rage. . _ _

"I cannot believe my uncle made such a request as that of his own free will," she cried. "I believe that you have forced him into making it, and I resent it most bitterly. Heaven knows I hated you deeply enough before, but now—"

"'Stop l" he cried, "you goad me too far. There Is a limit to even my patience and endurance. Repeat those words, and I swear to you I shall declare this marriage off. My next step will be to unmask the colonel, by placing him in custody of the officers of the law. Either submit quietly to the decree, or state that you refuse. It is becoming a matter of indifference to me, I assure you."

A piteous, wailing cry fell from the girl's lips. "Remember there is no coercion in this matter. You are at perfect liberty to do as you choose." 'You know I cannot but choose to submit," she sobbed, "for my uncle's sake." "Well, when can the ceremony take place 2" he asked, frowning impatiently. "It matters little to me," sie retorted, bitterly; " as good one time as another, since the cruel sacri- fice ?lOW he made." "Will to-morrow, at this time, suit you ?" he asked, brieily. She nodded, wearily: "I shall insist that my uncle and Miss Carris- court, my companion, be present." He turned pale to the lips under his dark, curling moustache. This was an unlooked-for dilemma which he had not foreseen. He was equal to the situation, how- ever. for he answered, instantly: "It is quite impossible to comply with your re- quest—for the colonel is confined to his room by his old enemy, the gout."
CHAPTER XXXIIL WHEN HE WAS WANTED HE WAS NOT THEBZ, lonic turned abruptly away, too proud to let him see am was tliat gathered is bat Ask eyes,

"If that is the ease, I have nothing more to say; said lonie, briefly—" no further objections to make. Make what arrangements you will. If my life must be spent with you, a day's or a week's respite will not matter much."

His eyes gleamed darkly as he looked at her. . How he longed with all his soul to tear away that barrier of cold pride behind which she had in- trenched herself and trample it beneath his feet, to drag this queenly girl down to his level. What a revenge he would take upon her for scorning him and his love so bitterly. He would make life one long torture for her—for
"Next to love, revenge is sweet," he told himself.

He settled it that the wedding should take place the following afternoon. "If you wish witnesses to the ceremony, imagin- ing I shall ever dispute it," he added, with a wicked laugh, "you can take these good. honest people, the Idalcolms, to the church with you." "I will have carriages to the door at three pre- cisely, in the afternoon," he said, rising. "Will that suit you ?" lonie bowed coldly. "Good afternoon, my fair lonie," he said, throw- ing her a kiss most gracefully from his finger tips, which she did not so much as deign to notice. "Rest assured I shall be punctual." It was not until after the door had closed behind him that lonie's courage, which she had made such an effort to preserve, gave way utterly. "Oh, God!" she cried, raising up her white hand, and sobbing to Heaven in the very fullness of her over-wrought heart, "would that there was no to- morrow for me. Why did you rescue me from the dark waters to doom me to a fate like this?"

There was a smothered moan and a heavy fall, which brought Mrs. Malcolm hurrying to the room with all possible speed. "The Lord have mercy l" she cried, with a gasp. "Miss Lawrence lying prone on her face on the floor, and in a dead faint."

Raising the slight figure in her strong arms, bole was taken back to her own room at once, placed in bed, and restoratives applied. Then the dark eyes slowly opened. "You fainted, my dear," said Mrs. Malcolm. I was afraid you were hardly strong enough to see any. one."

She wondered why the girl turned her face to the wall with as bitter a cry as ever fell from human lips. All night long lonie paced the floor of her room, crying out to herself that she wished the light of morning would never break. At last, day dawned pink and golden over the eastern hills, the birds sang joyously in the branches of the trees, the sun shone with a golden radiance on the waking earth—all nature seemed as joyous as though a human heart was not destined to be broken ere yonder sun should set.

"It is n2'ol:fling," murmured lonia, looking her hands tightly together as she stood by the window, "and my wedding day. Yes, ere yonder sun shall set I shall have been sacrificed as the price of my poor uncle's safety, his honour, and perhaps his life!"_ .

In her girlish, rosy day-dreams of the past— before this dark and awful shadow had fallen upon her—she bad wondered what her wedding-day would be like; for it is always the grandest epoch of a fair maiden's life.

She had pictured it all out to herself, as young girls will; how particular she would be over her toilet • how wondrous happy she would be; and how her heart would beat, her cheeks crimson, and her eyes brighten as the propitious hour drew near. Ah me those were only dreams. How different the reality was! _ _ _ _

Fate had parted her from the man she loved, and now she was to wed another, one whom she hated and feared. Without the bond of love between them, how desolate her future would be, and she thought o'.' the lines:

Is it sinful to gaze on the morning's sun, And with that the gates of the west it had won, That life's (lay was over and its labours done? Is it sinful in life no joy to take? To feel like a captive bound to a stake By a chain that galls us and will not break? Some fear to die; ' tis not so with me; Rather, oh, death, I pine for thee, And long in the quiet grave to be."
Great was Mrs. Malcom's surprise to learn of the wedding which was to take place that afternoon, and in response to lonie's invitation to come and witness it, she answered, heartily .

"Of course we will, raw dear." But in her own mind she wondered how her son would receive this startling intelligence. It so happened that when Frank Lyons had quitted the house the day previous, he had come face to face With William Malcolm, who was return- ing from the boat-house. Without deigning him so much as a glance, Frank Lyons, who was busy with his own thoughts, hurried quickly away. For one moment young Malcolm stared after him, as white as death. 'That is the man," he muttered to himself. "I said if I ever saw him again, I should know him, as sure as fate. I wonder if he wears a serpent diamond ring on his right hand? Yes, surely it is he. I could never, wver be mistaken." With breathless haste, he hurried into the house. "Mother I" he cried, breathlessly, as he came hurriedly across her advancing to meet him, " who is that man, and what did he want here ?"

"Now, my dear Billy," said Mrs. Malcolm, "why will you persist in asking more than one question at a time? As to who the gentleman is I cannot say. As to what he wanted, I can answer that be came in response to a letter which Miss Lawrence sent a day or so ago—the letter you yourself post.ed for her. I understood her to say it was a relative she was expecting." William Malcolm laid, a heavy hand on his mother's shoulder.

"I am sorry to hear that Miss Lawrence is in any way related to him," he said, slowly, "for he is a Villain, a rascal of the deepest dye. IS he had been —her—her lover, I should have warned her against him to have saved her from him at the cost of my life."

For long hours afterwards thoge words rang in Mrs. Malcolm's ears. They returned to her now with redoubled force as she received the intelligence that lonia was to marry him ; and it occurred to her, ton, that the prospective bride certainly did not look much elated over it.
"He is a very handsome young gentleman, my dear," she said, wistfully. "I hope he is as good as he looks."

Was it only her fancy, or did the girl shiver as with a sudden cold? But lonie made no answer. "It seems very sudden, my dear," she pursued. stopping short with embarrassment. Mrs. M.lcolm was most eager to tell the news to her son; but, as was generally the ease, whenever he was wanted he was not about.

He had left the house early that morning, and it was nearly noon now; still he had not come. "If he does not get in before we go, I will leave a note on the table for him, telling him where vie have gone," she concluded. , Slowly the hours dragged their slow lengths by. At length it struck three in measured strokes, or!,d the sound fell upon lonie's ears like a death-1' and almost simultaneously she heard the sound of carriage wheels. "God give me strength to go through it 4" was the the fervent cry that rose to Heaven &owe lips. The next moment she heard footsteps on the stairs, and Mrs. Malcolm looked in at the door. her p "Don't be a tardy bride, my dear," she said. "It's a had sign—it is, indeed. The young gentle- man is waiting, and Lot very patiently, if one may judge from the way he is pacing up and down. He has got two elegant coaches at the door, one for you and be and the other for Mr. Malcolm, my son William, and me; but, just as like as not, William won't be here in time to go with us. Are you ready. Miss LaWTOI2III.3 2"• "Yes," said lonie ; and in utter silence—though her heart was breaking—she followed her down to the room where Frank Lyons awaited her. "Do not speak to me," she whispered, as he sprang forward to meet her. "Do not touch me. If you do, I shall fall dead at your feet." So, in utter silence, he placed her in the coach In waiting, and toolihis place by her side. , (To be continued.)

div.head: CHURCH OF ENGL.,IID UNION..
div.p: CHURCH OF ENGL.,IID UNION..
ANNUAL MEIITING.

The annual meeting of the Warrington Branch of the English Church of Union was held in the Masonic Rooms, Sankey-st., on Tuesday afternoon. There were then present the Revs. F. Slater and W. 11. F. Waine, Chaplain to Colonel Legh, of High Legh ; Mr. John White (sec.), Mr. Bolton (trea.), the Mayoress, and other ladies. Toe chair was taken by the Rev. F. Slater. Letters of apology were read from the President of the Branch, Canon fleron,and the Vice-President, the Rev. E. D. Garvin, wno were both convalescent, but still unable to attend. Com- munications were also read from Mr. George Hearn, ot Liverpool, and Mr. George Egerton,of Warburton, the latter thanking the union for the vote of condo- lence passed to him and his family at the time of his father's death, and Mr. Burgess, and Mr. H. Wood.

div.head: ANNUAL RIPORTS.
div.p: ANNUAL RIPORTS.

Mr. John White, secretary to the Union, in his annual report stated that as no meetings had been held during the past year, chiefly in consequence of the illness of the President and Vice-chairman, he had no rec.,rd of im- portant business to submit. He had pleasure however in mentioning a word about what was called the Lincoln judgment. Although they might disapprove of the court 'rom which the judgment issued, it could not be but a matter of deep thankfulness that the court when appealed to by their opponents, had vindicated almost the whole of those practices which the English Church Union had been fighting for during the past quarter of a century. The number of members and associates of the Branch remained exactly the same as last year, namely, 83. They had lost a few as usual by death and removals, but just as many new members had joined as they had lost. Mr. Bolton, the treasurer, reported that the total receipts for the year were £6 10s. 10d. ; of that £8 2s.Bd.had been contributed to the general funds, and a balance of Bs. 2d. had been retained in hand.

div.head: ELECTION OF OFFICERS.
div.p: ELECTION OF OFFICERS.

The Rev. Canon Heron was re-elected as president, and the Rev. E. D. Garvin, vice-chairman. Mr. John White was re-elected secretary and Mr. Bolton was re-elected treasurer. The General Committee was re-elected. Mr. John White, in accepting office, said he did so for the Nit year. He had served as secretary for 23 years, and was anxious to resign ia the 24th year.— Tee Chairman said he was sure the great thanks of the society were due to Mr. White for re-accepting office, ana he had no doubt that they with him would hope that Mr. White would continue in office next year. (Hear, hear.) The CHAIRMAN in making a few opening remarks alluded to the great benefits which the Union had assisted in bringing about in the ritual of the church. He remembered when he was a boy going to festival— about the first connected with the Union—at Manches- ter, in St. Stephens Church. The service was con- sidered to be an enormously ritualistic one at the time, and when he looked back upon it there was no ritualism in it at all. It was a very plain celebration of the Holy Communion, and yet it caused the greatest commotion in the dis- trict, and brought down a considerable amount of odium upon the vicar of the parish, from the bishop of the diocese. On another occasion he remembered when there were in connection with St. Alban's, the incum- bent and a curate inhibited for a show of ritualism, and they had to sit amongst the congregation, whilst most of the service was carried on by the choir, and each indi- vidual had to say the prayers for himself. MI this was a great contrast to the ritualistic services which were conducted at the present time, and which had been brought about by the aid of the Church of England Union.—A paper was afterwards read by the Rev. H. F. Waine, upon the spiritual construction of the church as a body, and the architecture of the church as a building. The meeting was closed with the usual votes of thanks.

div.head: ANOTHER CHARGE OF INHUMANITY
div.p: ANOTHER CHARGE OF INHUMANITY
TO CHILDREN.

At the Warington Borough Police Court, on Mon- day, before the Mayor (Alderman Greenell), Alder- man Harrison, and Messrs. F. Monks, W. Pierpoint, and T. Birchall, the case adjourned from a month previous in which Thomas Mitchell, labourer, of Welsh's Yard, Latchford, and Celia, his wife, were charged with cruelly neglecting their children was heard. The male defendant did not appear. Mr. J. D. Buckton, appeared for the prosecution on be- half of the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children. He said the case was one of continuous neglect of the children, in not supplying them with sufficient food and clothing. They were in a most filthy I condition, so that at school it was impossible to put them with the other children. The man was in regular work at 235. a week, and the woman was earning 10s. a week. They had been severely cautioned, but the children were as much neglected as ever. The Society in these cases did not wish to prosecute unnecessarily. They acted upon the ground that prevention is better than cure, and took every possible step to avoid a prosecution.—lnspector Uphill deposed : On Tuesday, November Ist, he found the defendants' three children fairly clean and fairly well clad, but the house in a dirty condition, and no food except two slices of toasted bread. There was no one in the house but the children. On the 7th inst. he saw the chilaren at St. Mary's school. One of them, John, was very ragged and had on a shirt black with dirt and ragged. He appeared to be suffering from the cold. The other boy, William, was sent for by the schoolmistress. Be had neither boots nor stockings, and his legs were in a filthy condition, as if they had never been washed for a considerable time. He vent to the house and found the male defendant at the door smok- ing. He admitted that he had lost no sork ; and also that there was no food in the house, but said he was waiting for his wife to come home. There was no fire in the house, and it was in as bad a condition as before, and the kitchen windows were also broken. On the 14th inst. he visited the house again and saw John. His flesh was exposed through his clothes, filthy, covered with vermin, and his body emitted an offensive smell. William had vermin on his frock, and was black with dirt, also covered with flea bites. He was scantily clothed.—Ellen Dakin, 46, New- road, Latchford, deposed to finding the children crying with cold near her home, and taking them in and warm- ing them and giving the little one a jacket and some bread and butter. Both the defendants were very intemperate people.—Mr. Pierpoint 'remarked that the children did not look badly nurtured at all. He did not see the least evidence of starvation.—lnspector Uphill said there could be unnecessary suffering caused with- out starvation. The charge was neglect not starvation. —Alderman Harrison: Cruelty--The mother here uttered piteous cries, and protested that the children were not neglected, and were now well fed.—The Chief Constable You are not crying: you are only making a noise.—Some conversation took place between the Bench and Mr. Buckton as to sending the defendants to prison, and the children to the workhouse, and the mother with clamor- ous outcries implored the Bench not to part her children from her, or send her to prison. She admitted that the children had been formerly neglected., but assured the Bench that they had not been since her husband turned teetotaller.—The magistrates ultimately adjourned the case for another month, informing the mother that if there was no improvement in the treatment of the children in the meantime, the defendants would be severely dealt with.

div.head: TERRIBLE HOTEL FIRE.
div.p: TERRIBLE HOTEL FIRE.
TEN LIVES LOST.

FRANKFORT, WEDNYSDAY.—A disastrous fire has oc- curred at an hotel at Unna, in Westphalia, by which ten persons lost their lives. The fire originated in a drink- ing room on the ground floor of the hotel, and whilst endeavours were being made to pierce the walls in order to cope with the flames, the roof of the next building fell, burying a large number of persons. Among the dead were M. Brutkohl, the town architect, the hotel keeper, a sculptor named Simonis, and lour others, whose corpses were reduced to cinders. Three firemen also fell victims.
