div.head: EXAMINER, SATUPDAY, NOVEMBER 26, 1892. THE. LATE MR. JOHN WALKER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATUPDAY, NOVEMBER 26, 1892. THE. LATE MR. JOHN WALKER.

Tivs followiniz appreciative notice of the late Mr. Walker, the editor and proprietor of the " Examiner appeared in the Blackburn " Times " of Saturday, and is frpm the pen of Mr. Abram, formerly editor of the " Times i"—

"It is but d ati fill for us that in the columns of this paper, on which he worked some twenty years, and by the hand of one of his old comrades in this service some memorial of John Walker should be printed. A large proportion of those who will read it were sufficiently acquainted with Mr. Walker to know that nothing which may be written of his character, talents, and dis- interested devotion to the interests and welfare of the working people from whose ranks he sprang is insin.ere untruthful compliment, but that these goad qualities of our vanished friend are indeed inadequately pourtrayed. It is impossible to make tkis sketch exact or complete as to biographical particulars. There are no near rela- tives of Mr. Walker at hand to furnish such details ; SR that the writer has only his own general recollection of the main events of the history of his subject to fall back upon. The deeds of a useful and vr,rthy life are, however, much more to those left behind than the precise dates at which this or that ordinary incident happened. John Walker was born in Blackburn in the autumn of 1845. His father, Ea ward Walker ,was a working-man,. but amongst the mass of manual workers in these Lan- cashire towns appears many a man and woman of ex- ceptional intelligeace and mental energy, and one of such was Edward Walker. He was a representative man of the highest grade of his order—distinguished by shrewedness, honesty, independence of spirit, moral courage, sobriety, frugality, and plodding industry. Caring for his fellow-toilers, and possessed of special thinking and speaking powers, Edward Walker became a leader in the direction of the efforts of the operatives of Blackburn to protect themselves by union, and to im- prove their condition. He stood up bravely for their claims before the employers, but it is recorded as his peculiar merit that his counsel was always given fear- lessly for amicable settlement of disputes, and against unnecessary turnouts and strikes. Edward Walker 'died in middle life, killed by a fall in the dark, in the. engine- house of a weaving-shed, in which he and several other working-men had commenced cotton manufacturing. John was his only surviving child, and he cer- tainly inherited some of his father's distinctive traits. His mother (she was a Dobson), was a homely, but good , Christian woman, and she lived to see her son make, himself a force iis local journalism and a name in Lan- cashire literature. Old Mrs. Walker was proud of "- her John," and she found a home under his roof as long as she lived. She died in August of this year. Mr. Walker had not the advantage—if advantage it be—of an expensive, protracted course of education. He received the rudiments of knowledge in the day and Sunday schools of one of the churches in the town—St. Michael's, probably. Afterwards he attended a school carried on by a Mr. Sedgwick, and after beginning to work he attended classes in connection with the Mechanics' Institution. He went to work at an early age, and it was some kind of employment in the ware- house of a cotton- factory with which he started. The late Mr. Frank Johnston noticed the lad, and found him a place at Peel Mill. No kind of practical knowledge can come amiss to the journalist—he wants it all, at one time or another—and what John Walker in his youth ob- served of factory labour stood him in good stead in the discussion of labour questions as a public writer and speaker. But work in the warehouse and office of a mill was little to his taste. He was already studiously bent, and read the books within his reach with avidity. The literary faculty was latent in him. Half consciously he yearned for some employment which would enable him to cultivate that faculty. Some time about 1865 Mr. Ernest King. then proprietor and editor of the "Blackburn Times," engaged John Walker as clerk in this office, with the understanding that he was to practice shorthand and qualify himself for the duties of a reporter. Thus at the age of nineteen years, ! Mr. Walker entered a newspaper office, and began that connection with journalism which continued whilst he lived. His first duties were to rec-ive advertisements, keep accounts, and deliver papers on publishing morn- ing. From that be rose to paragraph writing and reporting ; then to sub-editing, eventually assuming the business management of the" Blackburn Times " ; and removing to Warrington eight years since to edit •the " Warrington Examiner" for Messrs. Toulmin, he finally a year or two later, took over the paper as pro- prietor. Few lads who commence in the lower positions on a newspaper are fortuned to ascend, as Mr. Walker did, step by step, through several responsible positions, to the goal of an aspiring journalists's ambition, the possession of an established newspaper. The latter is not perhaps altogether an enviable a chievement, in these times of remorseless competition and of transition in the English newspaper trade, but the position is at least one of potential influence upon affairs in public opinion proportionate to the extent of a newspaper's circulation.

In February, 1867, the " Blackburn Times "was pur- chased by Messrs. Toulmin, and Mr. Walker was en- gaged to continue in the situation he had previously filled. He was a clever, sprightly young fellow at that period ; liking society, where he could make himself agreeable and entertaining; sanguine and mirthful ; delighting in the stage, in music, in dancing ; but withal a still more ardent votary of Nature, worshipping her on mountain tops and on the merges of pellucid lakes and lonely tarns ; by waterfalls and winding rivers and in forests dim; and on the ocean shore. From first to last he was an enthusiast for scenery, for flowers and trees, and all descriptions of natural beauty. He surveyed them with the poet's eye, and received their inspirra- tion into the poet's soul. For John Walker was a veritable poet, and no " mute, inglorious Milton " of the village either. His muse had found a tongue and her accents were eloquent with true music—" the sweet, sad, music of humanity,"—whether she spoke in the refined English of the scholar and the gentleman, or in the strong Saxon of our north-country peasant. Some of Mr. Walker's songs and lyrics in the dialect of Lancashire are fit to compare for idiomatic expression and genuine native humour and feeling with those of Edwin Waugh, and that is saying a good deal. Of his favourite poets Shelley was perhaps first, and after him Tennyson, Byron, Beats, Wordsworth, and Burns. Amongst prose writers Emerson stood first in his estimation. Space forbids the citation here of even a few lines from some of Mr. Walker's happiest efforts in poetry, but many of his pieces are " familiar in their mouths as household words" to the "common people" of Blackburn, and of Lancashire. _ _

As a politician Mr. Walker was a Radical out-and-eut, and he entered into political agitation and controversy on the side he had espoused with all the earnestness and zest of which he was possessed. In fact, he gloried in debate, and revelled in word warfare. He was vastly more at ease and in his element delivering fluent speeches on the platform than nineteen out of twenty members of Parliament, candidates for that honour, and local chiefs of parties. In twenty years of active par- ticipation in the strife ef politics, in 131a.:kburn, Warrington, and the places around, Mr. Walker had abundant practice in public speaking, and he had attained great readiness and self-command. Some ten or twelve years since, when Parliamentary debating societies were formed in this and most towns, Mr. Walker was selected to lead the Liberal party in the local" House of Commons," and the party being more
numerous in the membership of the society than the Conservatires, v,ted itself into office, and Mr. Walker

became Premier, and " formed a cabioet.". The debates were condocted by both 'sides with ability and good order ;: an It k disp tragerriont of .thers to say that Mr. Walker was the best debater, if not the ablest set speaker, in the " House," and defended the policy of his " Government " with wonderful address and to the entire satisfaction of his colleagues and followers. In town's aff tirs, both here and in Warrington since his removal from Blackburn, Mr. Walker, as writer and as speaker, bore a conspicuous part, -and he stood by him- self ~s the independent champion of popular rights, and the trenchant denouncer of " jobs "'and exposer of long- standing abuses, fearless of men and of consequences, which were occasionally unpleasant to himself. Ile might have lived longer if he would have spared him- self and confined himself to his editorial work, but it was not in his nature to be silent, or to shirk the labours in the public behalf to which his sense of duty impelled _ _

If Mr. Walker commanded respect and admiration from those who watched his course as a public man, he was even more valued and loved as a private friend. In spite of his ailments, some of which had hung upon him a good many years, Mr. Walker's company was enter- taining in a rare degree. He was so vivacious, so hearty, so witty, that his conversation in the social circle was always delightful,, and brought out whatever was bright and good in others who were present. What pleasant country walks some of us have enjoyed with him, and how unforgettable are many incidents of our happy in- tercourse ! It is too saddening to think that those re- unions can never be repeated. His fidelity to his friends in their times of difficulty was noble, and greatly en- deared him to them. Passing differences of opinion never affected his friendship. About eighteen years since, Mr. Walker, who was then living in London, married Miss Jane Sandford, daughter of the late Mr. Ben Sandford, of Blackburn. Three children were born to them, of wham two, a son and a, daughter, are living. The engagement which Mr. Walker accepted in London did not prove to his liking, and after two or three years he returned to Blackburn, and to his old post, or to a more important one, on the "Blackburn Times."

Mr. Walker's views on religious subjects were not those which men who claim to settle what is truth in religion would call "orthodox." Perhaps the main difference between him and some who pass for believers was that he frankly avowed doubts and perplexities which all thinking men more or less feel,but many deem it prudent to keep to themselves. But his conclusions respecting a great First Cause and the imperishableness of the human soul were at least far removed from that bold atheism which scorns the conception of a God, or that dreary materialism which rejects the idea of a spiritual existence. Of this we are sure, that if there be a future life, John Walker's spirit is fitted to enjoy it in its fullest and purest potentialities. The lines from Shelley printed on his memorial card—were they chosen by himself ? we are comforted to think express his matured convic- tion with regard to man's destiny beyond the grave : " Peace, peace. he is not dead, he does not sleep: He hath awakened from the dream of life."

div.head: CURIOUS STORY OF A DREAM AT WARRENGTON. A REMARKABLE NARRATIVE.
div.p: CURIOUS STORY OF A DREAM AT WARRENGTON. A REMARKABLE NARRATIVE.

A curious story 01 a dream has, says the "Liver- pool Daily Post," gained currency in a country dis- trict adjoining Warrington. A young man, twenty years of age, was taken ill last spring with rheumatism, which ultimately took away his rea- son and rendered him prostrate and unable to walk. While in this condition he dreamed three times that he had to be conveyed in a big boat with two sticks to the Island of Arran, and that there would be big " lumps" on the sea. His friends were unaware of the existence of so famous an island, but they looked up an atlas, and, finding its whereabouts, they resolved to yield to the patient's phantasm, and take him by sea from Liverpool to Arran. All went well until rounding the Mull of Galloway, when boister- ous weather and a heavy sea were encountered. The pitching and tossing of the boat had the same natural effect on the patient as it would have on many persons in their normal condition ; but after the worst was over it was seen that for the first time there were signs of his reason returning_ When Arran was reached the youth insisted, in his half-conscious condition, on having a certain herb kept on his forehead for two days ; and this hallucination was also gratified. Whether as an effect of this or not, the result of the whole was that the youth's reason was restored. He is, however, still unable to walk.

Full inquiries by independent parties at the youth's home fully established the authenticity of the story. For three months his reason was gone owing to illness. The three dreams occurred on the nights of three separ- ate Fridays. On one occasion some years ago he sailed with his parents to Glasgow,. but nothing occurred to fix Arran in his memory, and his parents had to look at the atlas to find where it was. They put so much faith in his dreams that they went to the expense and risk of the trip, although their son was totally unconscious of where they were taking him to. He partially regained his reason on the voyage, but it was fully restored while in Arran, although at first he could not read. The other dream was to the effect that if his mother placed seaweed on his forehead he would sleep for an hour, and waken able to read. This was done, and sure enough at the expiry of an hour, his mother haying timed him with her watch, ha awoke, and was able to read a book, which was at once handed to him. The parties, who are thoroughly respected country people, returned from Arran on Saturday.

div.head: AMERICAN OPINION AND M‘KINLEYISM. '
div.p: AMERICAN OPINION AND M‘KINLEYISM. '
The following is an extract from a letter which has been received by Messrs. J. Pollitt and Co., of Manches- ter, from one of their correspondents in the ITnitcd States. The date is November 11:

The election is over, and I presume it Is no exaggera- tion to characterise the defeat we have administered to the Mliinley high tariff Republican party as a veritable "cyclone," a " land slide," a " tidal wave.' The way it looks at the moment, the party seems to have been left without a leader and without an issue, practically swept out of existence. It would not stop in its wild, reckless, corrupt high tariff legislation, so it has been stopped by the American people, who have risen in their wrath and might and declared "No further shalt thou go !" Well, the whole thing was a great surprise to us, for we tariff reformers did not believe that the people had been educated up to the right point ; but it seems we were mistaken. The farmers and working-men of the country, especially in the West where it was least expected, have at last got it through their thick heads that Protection does not protect them, and that it is one-sided, selfish, and ex- pensive. The rural and labouring vote was very significant and conclusive on this point. You may now confidently look for a return to common sense and a radioal reform in the present grotesque tariff of this country.

div.p: CA RD-TI AItPE RS SENT TO GAOL.

William Lloyd and Jabu Lowe, who were stated by the police to have carried on card -slia rue ng and other nefarious practices for years, were on Wednesday each sentenced at the Liverpool Police Court to three months' imprisonment for frequenting the streets with intent to eammit a felony. The prisoners when arrested had " flash " notes and bills of exchange in their possession, and it was proved that they had tried to work the con- fidence trick on a man in a public-house.

div.head: LABOUR COMMISSION. REFLECTIONS ON WORKNIEN.-THE ALKILI TRADE.
div.p: THE LABOUR COMMISSION. REFLECTIONS ON WORKNIEN.-THE ALKILI TRADE.

At Tuesday's sitting of the Labour Commission several witnesses were examined on behalf of the Central Association of Master Builders. Mr. Stanley Bird said that intis trade the ordinary workman paid by the hour did not do half the amount of work in the hour that he did thirty years ago. Being told by Mr. Mundella that this was a serious allegation, the witness repeated it, with the addition that the bricklayer, who used to lay 1,000 bricks in the day, did not now lay more than from 300 to 400 in a day of nine hours. Evidence was also taken from the alkali trade. Mr. Brock, chairman of the United Alkali Company, embrac- ing nine-tenths of the works in the country, asserted generally that the health of the operatives was equal to that of the average of men in other trades. He des- cribed the evidence which had been given on this point as sensational. Several of the Company's employes were called in corroboration of Mr. Brock's evidence.

div.head: SENSATIONAL BURGLARY NEAR LIVERPOOL.
div.p: SENSATIONAL BURGLARY NEAR LIVERPOOL.
EXCITING SCENE IN A GENTLEMAN'S GARDEN.

At the Liverpool County Sessions on Saturday, two middle-aged men, named Thomas Wilson and James Gatten, the latter being a corpulent man, were charged with committing a burglary at the residence of Mr. B. Heywood Jones, Larkhill, West Derby, on Thursday night last. Police-constable Hagan stated that at a quar- ter past nine o'clock on the night in question when go- ing his rounds he found a cord stretched across the path leading to Mr. Jones's house. He west round in another direction and saw a ladder placed against the balcony and two men at the top. He seized the ladder and tried to pull it away, but the men on the balcony endeavoured to prevent him, and threw a number of missiles at him, including a bedroom chair, but he was not severely hurt, and he got the ladder away. He blew his whistle and created an alarm, and the people in the house came to his assistance. The two prisoners were apprehended, hut a third man get away. A number of burglarious instruments were found on the prisoners and in the house, and the men are supposed to belong to a gang of professional burglars from London. lhey were remanded till Monday, the 28th inst.

div.head: "THE COMING WAIL!'
div.p: "THE COMING WAIL!'
PLAIN SPEAKING BY THE GERMAN CHANCELLOR.

Count Caprivi delivered an important speech in the German Parliament on Wednesday in bringing forward .the new Military Bill. He referred to the war of 1870, and read the original of the famous Ems despatch, in order to show, as he said, that Germany did not provoke the war and that Prince Bismarck had not falsified the despatch. Whilst disclaiming any idea of forcing the bill on Parliament by raising a " War in Sight " scare, the Chancellor said the Government felt the necessity of strengthening the forces of the Empire. The French " loved war for the sake of glory, and the more com- plete their armaments became the stronger was their self-consciousness and their desire for alliances, not for defensive purposes, but with the object of revising the map of Europe." Turning to the eastern frontier of the Empire, the Chancellor paid a tribute to the peaceful character of the Czar, but intimated that a powerful party in Russia was jealous of Germany. At present there was an " undesirable rapprochentent" between France and Russia, and their armies outnumbered the combined armies of Austria, Germany, and Italy. If Germany were attacked now she would fight at a dis- advantage, and the " men of 1813" would rise up and reproach their descendants if they did not make the necessary sacrifices to maintain what they had won. German' had lost the military supreinacv which she obtained in 1870 because the conquered had made greater sacrifices than the conquerors.

div.head: BLACKBD RN MURDER.
div.p: THE BLACKBD RN MURDER.
A VERDICT OF" WILFUL MURDER."

The inquest on the child Alice Barnes, who was 'mur- dered at Witton Park, Blackburn, on November 8 was resumed and concluded at Blackburn, on Tuesday, when evidence was given to the effect that the man Cross Duckworth, who is in custody, was seen running away from the scene of the murder at about the time when the crime was committed, and that afterwards two handkerchiefs were found in his house which were like the one which was taken from the murdered girl's mouth. The jury returned a verdict of wilful murder against Duckworth, who was committed for trial at Liverpool Assizes.

div.head: rRISONER BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: rRISONER BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

The accused, Cross Duckworth, was an Wednesday placed in the dock at Blackburn County Police Court and charged with the wilful murder of Alice Barnes. Mr. Backhouse appeared to prosecute for the Crown, and Mr. Riley defended. Mr. Baekhouse intimated that a day would be required to go fully into the case, and the bench remanded prisoner until Monday next for the pur- pose. Prisoner faced the crowded court with coolness, although he apparently lost a lot of flesh during his con- finement.. Before prisoner was taken below his solicitor referred in indignant terms to a paragraph in a local newspaper,. to the effect that neither wife, child, nor relative of Duckworth had evinced any interest in him since he was locked up. As a matter of fact a brother from Bradford and one from Tyldesley had instructed him, while his wife, who was almost heartbroken, was in court during the whole of the coroner's inquiry. He hoped such comment would now cease.

div.p: THE FIRST MAYOR AND TOWN CLERK OF WIDNES..

In the "Graphic" of Saturday last, there appear the pot traits of Mr. Allerman Fred ii.Glesage„l. first Mayor of Widnes, and Mr. H. S. Opp.-nheim, the first Town Clerk of the new borough. Both are capital likenesses, and appended are the followihg -lirtertirerdblls O'f cheir-respecrive cal era S F. H.Gossage,who has just been elected first Mayor of the newly-incorporated Lancashire borough of Widnes, is the head of the well-known firm of Wm., Gossage and Sons, soap manufacturers.. lie is the eldest son of the late Mr. Wm. Guseage, who was the first to seize upon the advantages off-Ted by Whine" in consequence of its unrivalled situation on the river Mersey, and its proximity to both the coal and salt fi-lds, for the erection of alkali works. Mr.Gossage has identified himself with almost every public movement in• Widnes, and was for several years chairman of the Local Board, the governing body of the town previous to its incorporation. He is a J.P.. for the county of Lancaster, and a member of the Upper Mersey Navigation Commission. His residence is Camp Hill, Woolton." The-portrait is from a photo by Messrs. div.head: CELEBRA.TION OF MR. J. J. CROSFIELD'S
div.p: CELEBRA.TION OF MR. J. J. CROSFIELD'S
WEDDING.. REMINISCENCES OF :THE SOAP WORKS:

On Saturday, the lang-deferred treat to Messrs. Crosfleld's workmen, by Mr J. J., Oros!leld, in cele- bration of his wedding, he having returned last week from his hymeneal tour, took place in the Bank Quay Mission Room. About 220 employ6s of the firm there sat down to a most substantial knife and fork tea, the caterer being Mr. John Willett, whose exertions for the comfort and refreshment of the guests were great, and the spread prepared by whom gave the greatest satisfaction.. After the tables had been cleared and removed, a most enjoy- able entertainment was given to the men, Mr. John Crosfleld presiding, and there being also present on the platform Mr. J. J. Crosfield, Mr. A. B. Crosfield, and Messrs. John Willett, W. Welsby, and J.. New- all.

The CHAnamal4 said they were very pleased to see them all there that night, and he hoped they had all bad a good solid feed that afternoon—(ap- plause)—and that none of them would be worse for it to-morrow morning. (Laughter.) He told Mr. Willett that he thought it would make the evening pleasanter if they were allowed to smoke, because it would not only give pleasure to a great many, but would also serve as a disinfectant during the present time of epidemic. The spread they had had that afternoon reminded him of a spread they gave 411 YEARS AGO in the works. It was on the occasion of a duty of £l4 a ton being taken off soap by Mr. Gladstone. (Ap- plause.) That was one of the great reforms he was proud to say Mr. Gladstone had brought about, en- couraging as it did, by making soap cheaper, the manu- facturer to improve his make, for formerly if he happened to make a boil of soap he had to pay £l4 a ton duty on it whether the make was good or bad, and if it turned out to be bad it had to go hack into the pans and the manufacturer lost his £14.. In those days the pans were locked down every night., and notice had to be given to the exciseman to unlock them next morning, before anythin,-; could be done. He did not know whether there was anyone present who could go back as far as 1847 when he first went to the works. He thought Abraham Lawton was there and would re- member—(a voice: " Get up Abraham," and applause.) They had then a

D4SMERNEABTA EXCYSIMAN, who did everything he could to annoy them, and his late brother was determined to be quits with him. By The law the exciseman could net look down a pan if there was any fire underneath, and what did his brother do but keep a man up night after night with a candle underaeath ?—(nauch laughter,)—and this poor miser- able exciseman had to march up and down—he could see him now—all night through. (Laughter.) His brother one day got a lead bullet and shied it through the window where the exciseman was sitting in his Little office. He was in a most fearful state of excite- ment, and went about the place saying he would give £5 to anybody who would say who shot at him. (Loud laughter.) At lust he petitioned to be relieved, and he was sent away (" Retired" and laughter.) After refer- ring to the increase of the works since those days-and remarking that there was a chance of increasing them still more, Mr. Crosfield observed that these meetings were good tor one thing, that was in bringing capital and labour, employer and employed, together, to their mutual benefit. (Applause.) It was the interest of both that the works should be prosperous, and every man ought to feel that it was his duty to do the best he could to support his master as the master supported the man. (Applause.) Before he sat down he should just like to say that they all had to lament the

MIRTH OF MR. ZORN WALKER. of the" Examiner." He was a man for whom he had the greatest respect. (" It is a pity ") a man of high principle and of great energy, and though he was afflicted with a disease which he knew must be fatal soon or late, in spite of all he stuck to his work, with an energy most praiseworthy, even to the very Ist. And they as Liberals of Warrington had to lament the loss of a man whose place would not be filled without great difficulty. He thought it was only right that he should refer to this that night, (Mr. A. H. Crosfield : Hear, hear), as his death was really a sad loss to the town. The Chairman in concluding expressed his regret that his wife and the bride had, owing to the horrible epidemic, not come ; otherwise,.he remarked, as they had told him, they would have been very glad to have been present. (Loud ap- plause.) Mr. WILLETT said it gave him great pleasure to stand onthat platform with theheads of the firm, and to join them in celebrating the marriage of Mr. J. J. Crosfield. He wished him and his wife

NTNIitY 10/' AND NAPPINNSB. (Cries of " Hear, hear.") He hoped their young master and his wife ...ould follow out through life the mottoes Bear ye one another's burdens,and Do unto others as ye would that they should do unto you. Referring to the presence of Mr. John Crosfield, the speaker remarked that it was not often he was seen at public meetings, but wherever his employ& saw him they would always feel that he had been to them a master whom they could honour and respect. (Ipplause.) Casting his mind back over the last 26 years he could say they had had many changes in the firm. He well remembered the time when Mr. George Crosfield and Mr. Morland Crosfield were with them, and although to-day they lay with the clods of the valley, yet he could safely say that they being dead yet spoke. After again referring to the pleasant relations between the employes and the present firm, Mr. Willett again wished Mr. J. J, Croslield every joy and happiness, and assured him of the hearty good wishes of all present. (Great applause.) Mr. J. J. CROSFIELD. who was received otirising,,with enthusiastic cheering, briefly and feelingly expressed his thanks on behalf of himself and wife, for these good wishes.

The entertainment during the evening consisted of piano performances by Mr. W. Johnson,.the accompanist and Mr. A. H. Crosfield, songs by Messrs. Stirrup and Grounds, recitations by Mr. Butterfield ;.a duet by Mn. Monks and Mr. Butterfield, a clarionet solo by Mr. Adcroft, and a most clever amusing ventriloquial per- formance with puppet figures representing Ally Sloper and his wife, by Mr. Grounds. On the proposition of Mr. Rhodes, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the caterer, which Mr. Willett acknowledged, and on the motion of Mr. G. Gleave, seconded by Mr. Taylor,the chairman was next thanked for his presence, and, Mr. A. H. CitosFIELE, briefly and happily acknowledged the compliment on behalf of his father. He remarked that he was glad to have the opportunity of expressing the pleasure it gave him to participate in these felicitations of his brother. Apart from the fact that they must all congratulate him on his good fortune, he thought it was getting high time— (laughter) seeing that he himself was such a hopelessly sluggish and confirmed bachelor—(renewed laughter)— that he should show that there was not wanting in one of the family that enterprise—(a laugh)—which to his mind was necessary before this important step was taken,. which, to quote an expression his brother had used that night, was like a leap in the dark. (Loud applause). A vote of thanks to the ladies and gentlemen who had contributed their services at the tea and entertainment was accorded. Subsequently the three Messrs. Crosfield accompanied the employes to the Bowling Green Inn, in the large room of which they niet,at Mr.J.J.Crosfield'S invitation. They drank his health, on the proposition of Mr. Willett, and with musical honounii, and enthueias- tic cheering for himself and his wife.—Mr. J. J. Gros- field, having briefly expressed his thanks, he and his father and brother took their departure, leaving.; their workmen to enjoy themselves in further convivialities.

div.head: WILL-MAKING IN CHINA.
div.p: WILL-MAKING IN CHINA.

From a report on Chinese wills, prepared by Mr. Watters, our Acting Consul General at Canton, it ap- pears that though the Chinese statute-book contains no reference to wills, the courts recognise them, and do not even require them to be in writing. If, however, they are mere oral declarations they must be made in the presence of witnesses, whereas written wills need not have witnesses at all. As a matter of fact, the testa- tor generally writes out his will privately, and then en- trusts it to his wife, or hides it away in some safe place. In theory a man in China may dispose of his property as he pleases, but this is based on the assumption that he will not do anything contrary to the dictates of reason and natural affection. Thus, a man may will away his property from his sons, but the court may set the will ' aside unless sufficient reason is shown. The most com- mon reason given is unfilial conduct. Chinese wills do not, it appears, knew anything of executors or admin- istrators. The legal representatives, with the assistance of senior relatives and the elders of the district, carry out the provisions of the will. In the interpretation of a will and in the carryine out of its arrangements, when there is any doubt or difficulty, it is the uniform custom to consult with the elders of the place. The final appeal, however, is to the Heal or other local autho- rity.

div.head: EXORCISING A DEVIL.
div.p: EXORCISING A DEVIL.
CURIOUS ACTION FOR SLANDER.

The Court of Eichtaed, in Bavaria, has given judg- ment in the action for slander arising out of an extraor- dinary ease of exorcism which occurred some months ago in Bavaria, when a certain Father Aurelian exorcised a boy named Zilk in his parish, who was said to be possessed of a devil. Father Aurelian declared that the evil spirit entered the boy's body through the witchcraft of a Protestant woman named Herz, and the latter accordingly instituted proceedings against him I for slander. The ceremony of exorcism was performed in the presence of a Capuchin friar named Wolf and other 'persons; and Father A.urelian,in a report which he drew up of the case,declared that the devil only quitted the boy after a long resistance.. Friar Wolf, who was one of a long list of witnesses called for the defence, confirmed the correctness of defendant's report as to the circumstances under.whieb the exorcism had been performed. Father Pruner, provost of the cathedral, who was called to give evidence as to the theological aspects of the matter, testified that, according to the teaching of the Church, the possibility of demoniac pos- session was indisputable, and he gave an account of the doctrine concerning demons and evil spirits. He declared that Father Aurelian had recognized signs of possession as taught by the schools, and had acted as he ought to have acted under the circumstances. After pointing out that even civil laws recognized the possibility of cove- nants between mankind and the devil, he went on to affirm that the Church could compel the devil to speak the truth. This was to support the line of defence set up by Father Aurelian that before quitting the body of the boy the devil, himself, speaking through the pos- sessed, had informed him that Frau Herz had bewitched the boy bymeans of some fruit which she had given him., Prior Schneider, who was summoned as an expert in demonology, also explained his views on the spirit world. A report was put in which was certified by the district supenntendent of Donanworth that the boy Zilk had no recollection whatever of being exorcised. Herr Straub (publi: prosecutor) thereupon observed that It was satisfactory that the Court was thus relieved of the necessity of pronouncing upon the efficacy of exorcism. The question before the Court was not whether Father Aurelia* had transgressed the law in exorcising the boy, but whether he had slandered the plaintiff. This, he maintained, defendant had don*, and he demanded damages to the extent of fifty marks, asking this small sum because it was not con- tended that Frau Herz had suffered any material loss by the allegations made against her. Frau Herz, in evidence, denied having bewitched the boy, and declar- ed that the fruit had not been given to Zilk by her, but by a maidservant. Her own children had also partaken of the fruit without suffering any ill effects. Ever since the slander spread by Father Aurelian, however, she had been called a witch, by the whole neighbourhood, ant' her children had been called " witch children " by their comrades in school. Ultimately the court gave judg- ment in accordance with the Public Prosecutor's demand, finding that Father Aurelian had uttered the slander, and imposing upon him a fine of fifty marks with costs, or five days imprisonment.

div.head: 'HIE EXAMINER,
div.p: 'HIE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 26, 1892.

Municipal A CLOSE obs4rvance ot the signs of I Affairs, the time is forcing upon the atten- tion of all thoughtful men, who are not blinded by their political feelings to the best interests of the town, the fact that the govern- ment of Warrington will, unless some measures are taken to prevent it, speedily be in the hands of men whose experience, abilities, and interests are of a very second rate order. In a large mea- sure the political character of the municipal con- tests which have occurred during recent years is responsible for the deterioration in the' person- nel! "of the members of our Corporation which has for some time past undoubtedly been taking place. This need not have been the case if each party had from time to time brought out the very best men in its ranks. Suvely, it ought to be considered an object of honourable ambi- tion by any citizen, however good his social position, to seek to become one of the " City Fathers." It is this spirit of local patriotism which has done so much to make the municipal institutions of our country objects of admiration and emulation to neighbouring nations. Has our town, to her wealthier and more cultured sons, ceased to be an object of any moment, except as a place for making money? Is there no responsibility upon those who—and in many cases their fathers before them—have " coined " money in Warrington, and now live miles away in sumptuous luxury, and surrounded by all the beauties of generous nature, leaving the workmen who have helped to build their colossal fortunes, entirely unhelped by the wealth, culture and intellectual ability, which ought certainly, in some degree, to be at the service of the town. Think for a moment of the number of wealthy Warringtonians who never lift a finger or a voice on behalf of any of our public institutions Our Museum, Tree Library, School of Art, Art Gallery and Technical Institute, all need and deserve substantial recognition, and yet, with one or two notable exceptions, no wealthy son of the "good old town" has, living or dying, done much for his birthplace. This, however, is only one aspect of the case. Our town not only needs some of the money of her wealthier citizens, but what just now is of far greater moment, she rag= • es the " brains " of those whose education and natural attainments most eminently fit them to be the "guides and philosophers" of our munici- pal politics. We are standing upon the threshold of a most momentous future. Questions of the very greatest importance, financially anel other- wise,and which—according to the manner in which they are decided, must materially affect the pros- pect of Warrington favourably or prejudicially— will soon come up for consideration and settle- ment; and while, on the one hand, the continued "absenteeism' of our more influential ratepayers I will inevitably result in disaster, perhaps deferred , somewhat, but none the less certain; o n h otker hand, their presence at the contributions to the deliberations of the Corporation upon these important questions would as certainly result in the greatest possible advantage to the whole com- munity. The oversight of our big "Bonded Debt," the construction crf our new streets and the widening of our old ones, the health of the borough, the control and management of the gas, water and sanitary works, the interests of War- rington as connected with the Manchester Ship Canal and the Arpley docks—these and kindred and equally important matters are in no sense affected by Imperial politics. Why, then, should not the political leaders of the town emulate each other in supporting only such]men as are known to be capable, honest, and free from self-interest?

IT will be agreeable news to the The Epidemic : Its Lesson. townspeople of Warrington to hear of the continued abatement of the smallpox epidemic. The loss which this visit- ation has caused to the town can only be partially calculated in figures. The ratepayers,. as a whole, represented by the Corporation, will have to meet a bill for extra expenditure which is not likely to be much less than three thousand pounds. In order to pay that bill an increase in the rates will be required for one year of little lees than six- pence in the pound. But the indirect losses sus- tained by sections of the community are still more difficult to bear, though not so easily reduced to a money value. There are few of the tradesmen of the town whose balance at the end of the year will not be adversely affected, while as regards those who have been personally afflicted or bereaved by the disease, their loss is not only serious from a pecuniary point of view, but distressing in its character. We have node- sire to indulge in recriminations as to the CatlBo of the epidemic. Many imputations have been more or less publicly made which are in the higheet degree unjust, and in not a few instance have been based upon ignorance. There has, in- deed, in some quarters been a remarkable mani- festation of that knowledge which comes after the event. But it is a worthless commodity. The supply is absolutely unlimited, while there are no useful or practical purposes to which it can be put. There can be little doubt that the genital/ authority have made mistakes in dealing with the outbreak, mistakes which would not be repeated if they had the work to do over again, with 00 benefit of the experience of the last few months. There was, for example,a slowness in realising the gravity of the outbreak, which is, it may be 1312&. pected, to some extent responsible for the unfor- tunate results which followed. But, while not wasting time with useless regrets as to the past, we should like to urge with the utmost emphasis that the epidemic has furnished one lesson of the greatest importance for guidance in the future. The lesson is that the sanitary condition of the town is not what it ought to be, nor what many people think it to be. The rapid spread in a community of an infectious disease like smallpox is in itself an almost infal" lible sign that there are some defects in the sani- tary arrangements. It should never be forgotten, too, that efficient sanitation is the only e ffectual and permanent protection against diseases of that character. We are told by a high autho- ' rity that no malady, once originated, has ever died out. The disease which formerly, under the name of the "Black Death," well-nig.,ll, depopulated this and other countries. stni lingers amongst us, it is said, as malignant typhus. The great "plague of Athens" is, it must be confessed, still too prevalent in the guise of scarlet fever; and the " plague of Con- stantinople," which raged in the fifth century,has, within the last twenty years, carried off hundreds of victims under the names of tetanoid fever and cerebro-spinal meningitis. It will be seen, there- fore, that it is not desirable to look upon these formidable maladies as matters of merely historical curiosity. If they are not now the des- tructive enemies of mankind that they used to be, it is because they are held at bay by modern knowledge and methods. Let a town relapse into its ancient state of filth and dirt, and it would quickly be decimated by its anciervt diseases, The farther it 0 removed from that state the more likely is it to enjoy an immunity from infection. Though in some respects the sanitary arrangements of War: rington are of an admirable character, the town ' has, as we have pointed out in these columns oa several occasions, its " Black Spots and insani- tary areas, which are a continual source of danger to the whole of the town. If the epidemic, which, let us hope, is now on the wane, has the effect of nerving the Corporation, which is the responsible party, to deal in a vigorous fashion with these possible centtes of iufection, the fl will not have been without its uses. the other hand,the policy of delay is still Pereisten in, a clear and, in some respects, a terrible lessow will have been ignored, and may, for all we kno ' be repeated in a still more undesirable form.

A Tory THERE is always a charm about the Remedy. unsophisticated Toryism of Mr' James LOWTHER, and no doubt it is because of this that a good deal of what ho has to say is widely published and road. Besides he often speaks out what others of the same political persuasion think, but have not the candour or courage to express. Mr. LOWTHER boldly Pre: pounds an all-round protection as the one anu only remedy for agricultural depression. But there is one rather singular omission from the letter which he has lately written to a meeting of agriculturists. He alludes to various demands which are made upon the diminished resources of the farmer, such as rates and taxes and profits 0f the middleman, but, in this connection, ho never mentions rent. Yet, Mr. LOWTHER is a land- owner and belongs to a family of landowners, and he must know that the claim which the farmer in straitened circumstances finds most difficult to meet is that of the rent a rent which nearly always includes a very large slice of "unearned increment." Mr. LOWTHER does not, indeed, altogether forgot to mention rent, but he couples it with the wages of the lab- ourer in a rather ingenious fashion. He advises those connected with the land to establish a vol- untary system under which rent and wages should be paid upon the selling prices of the various products of the land. "By such means," he adds, " all classes would become equally interested in restoring agricultura to conditions under which it could be profitably carried on." Think for a , moment of the pleasant prospect which such an arrangement would offer to the labourer. Let us take the case of a moderately large estate at a time when agriculture is in a fairly flourishing condition. On the one hand there is, we will saY • a considerable body of agricultural labourers employed by the farmers and severally paid a wage of, say, twelve shillings a week and twelve shillings a week is considered an excellent remuneration by this class of workmen in some of the counties of England. On the other hand there is the land- lord to whom the farmers pay rent to the extent of four thousand pounds a year. Then, we will suppose, there is a sudden and extreme fall in the price of agricultural produce, to the extent of fifty per cent. How will the " sliding scale" °f MT. JAS LOWTHER work under these circum- stances ? Naturally, people of " refinement " and " culture" will think with pity of the poor land- lord whose income has been suddenly reduced from something under eighty pounds to something under forty pounds a week. Be will perhaps be under the dire necessity of ordering a cheaper brand of champagne, or even have to dis 7 pense with a superfluous menial or two. But wha4

bout the agricultura labourer who had,by means of Mr. LOWTHER'S equitable contrivance, become "equally interested " with the landlord in the con- dition of agriculture ? The problem with which he would be suddenly faced would be " How to live on six shillings a week ? " Now, experience has proved over and over again that, by the constant schooling of necessity, which, as we are told, is 4` the mother of invention," a man may rear a family, with more or less discomfort, on twelve shillings a week; but to rear one on six shillings, week is beyond the wit of even an agricultural lal4ourer. Mr. LOWTHER'S plan of dealing with -agricultural depression is, therefore, worthless and impracticable. He deals with the question exclu- •sively from the landlord's point of view, and as -though the one sacred thing was rent. As a matter of fact it is in a diminution of rent that the farmers must, in the main, look for relief from their immediate difficulties, and for the permanent improvement of agriculture—which is after all, the greatest o our industrips—it is nnt likely that anythii.;..: short of a drastic revision of the tenure cf Lita will be suffici eat.

AVE paid the Conservative party of Warrington an unmerited compli- ment last week when we assumed that the contest in St. John's Ward was being •forced I.`t tileiii by an irresponsible member of the party. It seems, after all, that Mr. SHAW is the pary n,, 'deft and will be supported by the party machinery. This, it is needless to say, is a very flagrant breach of the letter and the spirit of the compact that was entered into by the two parties prior to the first of November, to avoid eine tion s in consequence of the prevalence of gmallpx. So obvious is this and so undesirable do sonic Tories find it to lie open to so injurious an imputation that we have heard it said that the contest is really being entered into rainst the wishes of the leaders of the party. But, then, the leaders of a party are thcse who lead, and it is quite evident that who- ever eau inanipalate an election are the real leaders. The nominal leaders may, for anything we know. have abdicated their position, or they may have been evicted ; or—for there is still another alternative—they may have' retired" for this occasion only. As far as those who are out- siders and do not understand the inner wheels of Conservative management are concerned, all that they know is that lecal Conservatives entered into an arrang nnent not to contest the municipal elec- tions this November because of the " prevalence cif smallpox," and that that arrangement has now been vi 0.0.:ed when there is a possibility of a Liberal•sqt being snatched. It has been said, `too, that the arrangement did not include .vacaneie3 that mlght be can sed by the election of aldermen. That is, however, one of the shabbiest and flimsiest oF subterfuges. These vacancies are part and parcel of the November elections, and it -was fully expected at the time the arrangement was made that a successor to Alderman BURGESS I would be chosen from the Liberal ranks. But apart from this, what was the meaning of all the protestations of .a desire not to spread the infec- tion by means of a contested election ? Were these all nothing but hypocritical pretences con-

cocted in order to get their six councillors again ,safely installed in the Town Council ? The epid- emic still prevails, and we believe there are more cases in St. John's Ward now than there were at the beginning of the month. Yet this is the time when a needless contest is forced upon the Ward and the health of the inhabitants is to be endanger- ed by the turmoil and movement of an election. We should strongly urge not only upon all Liberal 'voters in the ward hut also upon all others—and we are disposed to think there will be not a few—who resent the manner in which this election has been forced upon them to vote for Mr. MouN- FIELD, the Liberal candidate. Though there are
other two candidates in the field the contest will

really lie between him and Mr. SHAW. Of Mr. lhooLn little can be said. His chief claim to recognition is that he has formulated a mysterious ' scheme for dealing with the depots. So far as we have seen Mr. BYRNE does not claim to represent any one in particular. It has been said that he is the nominee of a body of Irish voters in the ward, but it will be seen from a report which we pub- lish that a meeting of Irishmen held last night unanimously decided to support Mr. MOUNFIELD.

THE trial of the notorious COOPER terminated on -Monday at the Isle of Man, in a verdict of mall- -slaughter by the jury, and the pronouncement of a sentence of ten years' penal servitude by the first Deemster or judge. Most people will be of opinion that COOPER has been dealt with in an extremely lenient fashion, and it is not surprising to learn that both the verdict and the sentence were greeted with a display of popular indignation. It seems, however, that criminals against whom the capital charge is preferred are not harshly -dealt with in the Isle of Man. The case before that of COOPER was that of a man named KELLY who had also killed his wife by nearly cutting her head off with a 'razor. He, too, escaped with a sentence of ten years' penal servitude. Manx jurymen are evidently not of a stern or vindictive character. It appears from an interview with one of those who sat in the COOPER case that the jurymen are well treated while discharging their judicial duties. The juryman in question spoke in laudatory terms of the "accommodation at the hoteband of the ex- cellent food and drink that was supplied to them."

_ Under such pleasing conditions, it was perhaps natural that they should look benevolently even upon a man who had stabbed his wife. Coomm, itis true, was a drunkard and a bully, but, on the other hand, he was wealthy and well connected.

Fr is amusing to note with what an air of offended virtue the Tory scribes and pharisees, local and otherwise, are holding up their pious , hands in holy horror at the sacrilege which the Chancellor of the Duchy has committed in his , recent appointments to the various Commissions of the Peace. The Chancellor's crime consists in recognising the public services of certain men who happen to be Liberals, by offering them the honour in question. Of course, the Tory party, who are responsible for a very considerable num- ber of the magistrates who adorn our local Bench, never for a moment allowed such b. thing as " politics "to affect their selections from time to time. They—the Tory party—have always been governed in their choice by the superior abilities, unquestioned integrity, sterling honour, intellec- tual calibre, high moral personal character and • socia fitness of the men whom they have selected. At least, if this is really not the case, certain local Tories, who \ forget that people's memories are am-net-idles unpleasantly retentive, wish us to be- lieve that it is. Now, let us see what the Tory party really has done in this important matter. But first we will go back to the period 1880 to

1885, the Liberal party being in power during those five years. Eleven magistrates were ap- pointed, of whom eight were Liberals and three (Aid. S. Cbandley, Dr. C. White, and Major Pick- mere) pronounced Tories. In the following period —lBB5 to IB92—during which the Tories had matters ehtirely in their own hands—fourteen magistrates were appointed, every one of whom, with one exception, is an uncompromising Tory and a etrong partisan. The Tory party in War- rington needs a great deal of purgation before its scribes can claim the right to criticise the actions of their opponents.

On Monday at Runcorn Petty Sessions, a platelayers' ganger named William Goodwin, employed on the Ship Canal, and residing in one of the huts at 13igfield, was charged with assaulting his wife, Jane Goodwin, on the 16th inst. Defendant, it was alleged, had assaulted his wife on several occasions previously, and on the day in question he knocked a number of her teeth out. The defendant said the prosecutrix had provoked him to assault her. She was continually running him into debt, and the children had not a change of clothing. They had been separated before, but she came back to him again. Prosecutrix was now living with another man. The bench fined defendant as. 6d. and costs for the assault, and granted a separation order, defendant to have the custody of five children, and contribute is. towards the support of the youngest child, which was left under the care of the mother. BREAKING A PUBLICAN'S ARM AT WIDNES. On Monday, at Widnes Police Court, Joseph Bradley, no fixed abode, was charged with doing grevious bodily harm to Samuel Hurst, landlord of the Commercial Hotel,Appleton. Superintendent Keighley said prisoner went into the hotel on Saturday night and commenced to misbehave himself. The landlord's wife remonstrated with him, and then Hurst came in and spoke to the prisoner, who said he would knock his eye out. Hurst then went towards the door to eject prisoner, when the latter caught bold of him, threw him on the ground, and kicked him in such a manner as to break his arm and injure him internally. Dr. Edwards was called in to see Hurst OR Sunday morning, and on examination found that his right forearm was fractured, and he was also afraid that he was injured internally. He was in a very weak state, and would not be able to appear for a week. The prisoner was remanded for that period.

At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, before Mr. J. Birchall and Mr. H. W. Deacon, two young men named Peter Houghton, of no fixed abode, and William Sproson of 12, Bank-st., were charged with stealing m fro the flat " Safeguard " a pair of marine glasses, trousers, &c., the property of John Whitehead. They were further charged with stealing from the Sit "Annie," a jacket and cap, the property of Samuel Summerfield ; from the flat Bertie, a pair of opera glasses, knives, &c., the property of Ralph Ravenscroft ; from the fiat " Lottie Maud," a pair of trousers and a cap, the property of William Dutton; and from the flat "National," one jersey, the pronerty of William Hurst. The robberies had been carried out over a considerable period, and suspicion fell upon the prisoners, who were apprehended, a considerable portion of the property being found in their possession.—The Bench imposed a fine of 20s. upon each defendant, or 14 days in default. 'The other charges were dismissed, the magistrates thinking the penalty in the first case sufficient punishment as they hal prisoner detained in custody a fortnight. Yesterday, Sproston was brought up at Runcorn Police Court, on suspicion of stealing a jersey, but as there was no prose- cutor, he was discharged.

Before Mr. Birchall and Mr. Deacon, at Widnes Petty Sessions, a labourer named John Wynne of Ditton, was brought up under two warrants dated respectively Jan. 17th, 1890 and Jan. Ist 1892, charging him with neglect of family.—Mr. Knowles defended, and in reply to him, Mr. Wood, relieving officer, admitted that he had not his authority to prosecute under the first warrant, and , the Bench decided that thay could only deal with the socond.—Mr. Wood said the prisoner left Ditton in 18E8, leaving his wife and three children, and in Jan. 1890 they became chargeable to the common fund of the Union. The Guardians had paid £24 6s. 3d. in outdoor relief.—Mr. Knowles defended, and said the case was a very sad one. The prisoner was driven from home by his wife's intemperance. The wife deserted her children soon after the prisoner went away and being a young woman she was able to support herself. The prisoner left his childrenin the care of his father and mother, who were then in good circumstances, but their means ia.d become reduced. The prisoner was not aware of this until recently, and he had returned from South America, where he had been, in order to support his parents.—Mr. Wood, in answer to Mr. Knowles, said he e.,uld not accept an offer of 2s. per week to clear off the debt—The Chairman said the magistrates considered it a very bad case. The prisoner had every opportunity of sending money over from Buenos Ayres, but he had not done so. He rauet go to gaol for a month's hard labour.

div.p: DEATH OF MRS. BUCKLEY, OF BELTONNITEOGOL,

On Wednesday, at Runcorn Cemetery, the remains of Mrs. Mary Buckley, wife of Mr. Edward Bitckiey,. otfl Halton Brook, Runcorn, were laid to rest. Tfre deceased,. who was 61 years of age, died after a brief illness. For a prolonged period she was an active worker in connec- tion with Halton Church and Holy Tfinity Church. Runcorn, and took a deep, active, and prominent part in, various evangelical movements. ID all she did she dis- played an unostentatious Christian spirit, .and ,her. death will be greatly mourned. The funeral was atterisied, by Dr. Preston and the Rev. A. Riley, in .addition to the relatives and friends. 'File obsequies were performed by the Rev. G. D. Wray, vicar of Halton.

An extraordinary difficulty has arisen in connection with this election. In the ordinary course of. matters the election should have taken place on Saturday,. Decem- ber 10th, but Mr. J. Ashton, clerk to the Union, the returning officer, has not received the reqpisite autho- rity from the Education Department. Mr. Aehton coat- municated with the Department on Tuesday,,and he has received the usual stereotyped replY, that the matter will receive consideration. The date of the election, is therefore in doubt. Prior to the electionAhreelears ago the contest had been held in Christmas .week,, but this was found a most inconvenient time, And the date, with the consent of the Department was, changed to the lOch December. Probably the officials have overlooked the change in the date.

THE POACHING ;AFFRAY AT BOLID.. On Thursday, at Widnes Petty Sessions,, .Ibha Row- son, of Warrington, was charged with poaching on Bald estate at midnight on Monday, the 14th inst. The estate is in the occupation of Mr. Wyatt,but Mr. Gcl. VVarren, ship owner, of Liverpool, LS the owner of, the shooting rights overthe land. Mr. .1.1 W. Knowles prosecuted, and Mr. A. Browne defended. . The bead keeper, Harry Davies, and two other keepers, were out watching in Bold Park on the night in question, when they came across three men netting for rabbits and a desperate fight with bludgeons took place. Davies was rendered insensible by a blow on the head, and the other keepers were also injured. Two ()Mile men escaped,, but the prisoner,who had been stunned, was captured. Davies who had six severe wounds, on his head, was an inmate of St.Helens Hospital for a,week. Sevewprevious convic- tions were proved against the prisoner, who pleaded guilty, and he was fined MO' and costs:end /9e. Si., or in default two months' hard labour, The nets and pegs were ordered to be forfeited. FUNERAL ,OE dS,RUNCORN VOLUNTEER. The mortal remains of Mr. John Ravenscroft. of Port- land-street, Runcorn, were committed to the grave on Monday, in ale unconsecrated portion of the cemetery. The deceased who was the son of Mt. Samuel Ravens- croft, sail maker,,&c., died on Friday after a prolonged illness and he leaves a widow and two sons and two daughters to mourn his loss. Mr. Ravenscroft was a gifted musician,, being able to play almost every kind of instrument, and his services were greatly in demand at all public functions. He had occupied the position of organist at Holy Trinity Church, Halton-road Wesleyan Chapel, and Bethesda Congregational Church. He had been connected with the VOluntser Band from its forma- tion, and his funeral partook of a military character, a number of volunteers preceding the hearse, which was followed by relatives and a large number of townspeople. A firing party under the command of Sergeant Woodland discharged three volleys over the grave. The funeral service was conducted by the Rev. T. Wilkes, Rev. W. Arrowsrnith, and the Rev. Dr. Preston. The Volunteer Band played the Dead March es route to the cemetery. RUNCORN SONS OF TEMPERANCE.

In connection with this society, a well attended meet- ing was held on Saturday evening, under the presidency of Mr. Thomas fleesom. An interesting essay on Oliver Cromwell," was contributed by Mr. Thomas J. Holt. Be referred to the stirring, events that bok place in the reign of Charles I, and the difficulties that mon- arch experienced in getting money from Parliament. Mr. Holt stated that Charles firmly believed in the divine right of kings. He went on to show that free- doom of speech was not then enjoyed,and described the fearful punishment men had to undergo for expressing their opinions. He gave a biographical sketch of the life of Cromwell, followed him through the various battles in which he had engaged, and alluded to the way in which he put down insurrection in Ireland, but stated that he was unprepared to defend the brutality exercised, which showed the spirit of the times. His refusal of the crown was also mentioned, and ref(ssince was made to Cromwell dying, comparatively spes,king,a poor man. The reading of the paper was succeeded by an interesting discussion, in which the folloning mem- bers engaged :—Messrs. E. Key, David Smith, Thomas Cooke, S. M. Timoerley. James Bisbrowe, Geerge E. Sutton, and David Bisbrown, A vote el thaßki Ws<S accorded to Mr. Bolt.

In alluding to the subject of "flar poorer church people," the Mural Dean made a feet remarks which were evideotly intended to have their effect at the approaching School Board election. Fre drew a picture of Roman Catholics having greater privileges than the church, itt regard to religious education in workhouses, though he was careful to say that it waonot in Runcorn Union that such a state of affairs existed. and went on to observe that if school boards became, compulsory and all denominational schools were abolished, then children would be co-rape/led to go to these 3tih,ol Board schools, and would be forbidden to have the religious instruction of their owe church given to them irs conjunction with their ordinary education "while others. may not be com- pelled and treated in the same way.'," It was high time they understood this matter, and saw that it was really a question of religious liberty. This. picture of a down- trodden State Church, the embodireest of privilege and ecclesiastical power, is much more amusing than it is startling. Does. the rev. Canon honestly believe that when school boards do become universal, the legislature will malts exception in the case of Catholics, or Wesleyans, ,or any other noncon- forming body, and allow them toteoch their distinctive doctrines to children in "conjunction with their ordin- ary education," while the all powerful church with its wealth and influence will be relee.Clessly crushed and forbidden to teach its creed ? Qtannon sense forbids. No, it is an attempt to frighten, the ratepayers into returning a majcrity of denominationalists to the school board by a bogie,which a moment's consideration would show in its naked absurdity, and leave only a feeling of surprise that a gentleman of the Canon's intellectual attainments and estimated knowledge of humanity should ever have put it forth.

Religious liberty, forsooth I! The vicar must go to his Nonconformist brethren if he wishes to know what it is to suffer ander pains and penalties, and yearn for reli- gious liberty. It is within the memory of living man that a man unwilling to go .be.church, and receive the sacrament could not fill any office under the crown; ; when to be a Dissenter meant that one was accounted." unworthy of appointment to the most insignificant-1 office, or the most obscurs• place, with which eitheaH honour or pay was connected_ Even at the present.dap, there tre two civil offices which are not free to all, and these are the offices of Lord Lieutenant of Ireland and Lord Chancellor of England. There are people yet alive in Runcorn who have vivlci memories el` the days when dissenters were compelled to pay a rate for the Chum'', against their consciences. Nay, it is too ridiculous to even imagine the day coming when the church with not have equal privileges tWth other denominations. But then one never knows what the whirligig of time,may bring.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
Ta-r OF WOOL.

At Monday's Warrington Borough Police Court, Michael Griffin, labourer, Bostcck-st., was charged with stealing on Saturday evening, a quantity of wool, the property of Mr. Pemberton, 35, Winwick-st. He was seen to go inside the porch of the shop and take the wool, and P.C. Leathwood being informed, apprehended him with the wool upon him.—The prisoner : I got a few glasses of whisky, and I was not reeponsible.—The Chairman : You have been here before.—The Prisoner: If you will look into it this time.—The Magistrates' Clerk : We are looking into it. A fine of 10s. and costs was imposed. STEALING OYSTERS BY A TRICK. Thomas Llewellyn,aged 24, labourer at the Whitecross Works, was charged with stealing, on Saturday night, by means of a trick, a quantity of oysters, the property of Thomas Shuttleton, 4, Pinner's-brow--It appeared that the prisoner went to the prosecutor's shop about ten minutes to eleven on the night mentioned, and asked for three pennyworth of oysters. A lad handed them to him, and he swallowed them, and was walking away. Shuttleton followed him for payment, but he declined to pay. Information was given to P.C. Bell, who arrested him near the Rodney public-house. He denied knowing anything about the oysters.—Mr. Monks : What is the trick /—Alderman Harrison : He swallowed the oysters.—He was fined ss.

div.head: FAINIILT SQtrAMILB.
div.p: A FAINIILT SQtrAMILB.

Mary Quinn, a married woman, of the Old-road, was summoned for assaulting her sister. Margaret Burke. The evidence showed that the affair was a family squab le. Defendant said it arose this way : lam a widder wid six children, and my sister, who is married, sends around for me pans, kettles, brushes, and the devil knows what. She sent her chaild for a brush and I sent word back that the last brush was used up out of me house, and oi wouln't lend another, win there was a row." The case was dismissed. " VERY CHOICE." "

John O'Neil, of Liverpool, was Sent to jail for one month on Friday, for stealing a ham from the shop of Edward Green, grocer, Buttermarket-street, the previous day. D.S. Monaghan was going along Buttermarket- street when he saw the prisoner strolling along with a broad smile on his face, and a bulging lump under his coat. They both stopped and looked at each other. Presently Monaghan said " Where are you going ?" " Whoana." Then he said that lump under his coat looked strange. Indeed it looked funny. But O'Neil said it wasn't funny. He said it was " tommy." So Monaghan said he would like to cast his eyes upon some " tommy," and he actually pulled it from beneath O'Neil's coat. And lo and behold ! It had assumed the shape of a large ham with a label upon it, which said " very choice." When the Bench sent O'Neil to spend a month at Strangeways they said it was rather a step not in accordance with O'Neil's choice.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
SLTURIDLT.—Before Mr. J. Burgess (in the chair), Aid.

, Chandley, and Mr. Volley. AFTER MANY DAYS.—Thomas Flarte. Bostock-street, was 'charged on a warrant with not having appeared to his summons for being drunk in charge of a horse and cab at Warrington, on the 7th of July, 1890. Defendant pleaded not guilty. P.C. Evans stated that on the night of the 7th of July, 1890, he saw the defendant in Sankey-st.drunk in charge of a horse and cab. He took the defeadant back to the Patten Arms Hotel. The defendant now stated that he was not drunk, and that he went to Stretton after going to the Patten Arms. The constable stated that this was not true, as the defendant was immediately discharged by Mrs. Kiernan. A fine of 56. and costs was inflicted. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Greenall), Alderman Harrison, and Messrs. F. Monks, T. Birchall,

and W. Pierpoint. • ASSAULTS ON CONSTABLRS.—Thomas Boyle, was charged with being drunk and disorderly on Saturday night, and assaulting P.C. Meacock, and doing damage to his coat and whistle. 'fhe officer said the prisoner by his dis orderly conduct was causing a crowd to collect in Peter-street, and he ordered him away. He went, but while witness was dispersing the crowd, came out, of his house, and attempted to strike him. A struggle ensued, and the prisoner tore witness's coat and damaged his whistle. The prisoner was fined 10s. and costs.---John Ward, a soldier on furlough, from Alder- ' shot, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Peter-street, on Saturday night, and assaulting Police- Sergeant Swab. The officer said he arrested the prisoner on account of his drunken and disorderly behaviour. He became very rough and violent, and witness had to whistle for assistance, and another con- stable came. The prisoner struck witness in the eye, and blackened it, also in the forehead, and kicked him "right and left" and threw him to the ground. He kicked him all the way to the police station. He .was fined 10s. and costs. TOSSING FOR MONRY.—John Bedderd, labourer, and Thomas Cowley, Manley-street, William Houghton, jun., Leicester-street, and Thomas Badger, Howard-street, all youths, were fined is. each for playing at pitch and toss for money on Sunday. CHIMNEY ON FlRE—Arthur Taylor, pork butcher, Irlam-street, for having his chimney on fire, was fined 53. DRUNlL.—Michael Morris, drunk on Friar's Green, the previous afterneon, was fined ss. and E. J. Guest.

Pa rrington , Pierpoint-street ; Mary Hugh, Church-street; James Hannigan, Buckley-court ; Wm. Dennett. BPswick-street ; James Longshaw, Mill-street ; CHARGE AGAINST A DOMESTIC SEilvANT.—Rate Carey, a domestic SPI'W nt, who lives in Bakehouse-yard, was charged with stealing 30s. from the houso of her master, Mr. Peter Rigby, 21, Ilowley-lane.—On Tuesday morn- ing last the prisoner was sent out on an errand, between eleven and twelve o'clock. As she did not return the suspicions of her mistress were aroused ; a search was made, and it was discovered that the money had been stolen. Information was given to the police, and Detec- tive-Sergeant Monaghan found the prisoner in Manches- ter, and brought her back to Warrington.—The case was remanded to enable the police to make further inquiries into the matter. Prisoner was brought up again on Wednesday, and after being severely spoken to by the Bench was ordered to be detained in the bride.ell for two days, and a conviction was recorded against her.

• WEDNESDAY. —Before 'Messrs. J. Fairclough (in the chair), J. Cieddes, and S. Wright. DRUNIKENNES3.—BodeIia Knoikton, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Itutterniarket-street the nrevious night.—Mr. Hunt said the audacity with which the defendant came up was appalling. Everything had

been done for her, and nothing would do her any good except an" iron rod."—Mr. Taylor,Police Court Mission- ary said he tcok her to Father Nugent's at Liverpool. She asked to be released, because she had a husband and four children in Warrington.—The defendant: "f wasn't going to stop there and be clemmed." Fined 10s. costs. —Ellen Connor was charged with a similar offence, and fined 10s. and costs.—Pelina Oultrim, who was also charged with drunkenness the previous night, was fined 10s. and costs. It was stated that she had two children in the hospital, suffering from small-pox. FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison (in the chair), Alderman Wright, Councillor H. Roberts, and Messrs. William Pierpoint and S. Wright. THE DIFFICULTY OF REGISTHILINO A "NEW ADDITION." —Ernest Hyde, of Liverpool-road, a railway clerk, was charged with unlawfully refusing to answer certain questions, to the officer of births and deaths in connec- tion with the birth of is child Sydney.—Prisoner pleaded guilty. Mr. Sutton prosecuted on behalf of the Board of Guardians, and stated that the defendant, contrary to the laws concerning the registration of births and deaths, refused to verbally answer questions put by Mr. Harrison, registrar of births and deaths in the Warrington district. , Defendant had offered written evidence to the registrar, but he was told that this was illegal and could not be accepted, as no written evidence except that of a coroner or a medical man was allowed by the law. The paper in the first place did not answer certain relevant questions, and upon tkis being explained to the defendant he be- came abusive and rude, and absolutely refused to an- swer questions put to him. He also acted in an unfair and impudent manner. For the offence he was liable to a penalty of 40s. and costs. Mr. J, Harrison, registrar of births and deaths, in Church-street, gave evidence to the effect that on the sth of November defendant came to his office and threw down upon the table a paper con- taining some few particulars respecting the bi rth of his child. Among other things which were not noti- fied was the defendant's wife's maiden name, and de- fendant refused to answer as to these.—Other evidence showed that the defendant wrote the paper with the best of intentions,but during a dispute about its legality Mr. Harrison threw the paper in the fire. This annoyed the defendant, and when Mr. Harrison asked any ques- tions of him, he referred him to the paper.—Alderman Harrison said the affair was a piece of obstinacy on the defendant's part. Defendant was fined ss. and costs.

A WEAK CHARGE.—J. Marsh was summoned for furious driving in St. James's-road, Latchford, on Monday night.—P.C. Evans stated he saw the defendant 'driving a horse attached to a spring cart. The animal was being driven at a furious rate, and the defendant when called upon to pull up refused.—Evidence was given by Mr. Mainwaring, auctioneer, and Mr. F. Wilkin- son, fustian cutters, was summoned for absconding from her employment.—lt was stated that the girl's parents were poor, and she had been sent to sell celery in the market to raise money each day for food.—A compul- sory order for the girl's return was made.

div.head: DOMINION OF CANADA.
div.p: THE DOMINION OF CANADA.

In another column will be found the advertisement of the Canadian Government calling attention to the advan tages offered to settlers in the different provinces of Canada. In addition to the free grants of land, and the improved farms that are to be bbtained at low prices in every part of the country, money bonuses are given to actual settlers upon the land in Manitoba, the North West Territories, and British Columbia, within eighteen months of their arrival. The pamphlets iasued under the authority of the Imperial and Canadian Govern- ments include an official handbook of informatien. and the reports of the Tenant Farmers who visited Canada in 1890 and 1891, and are well worthy the perusal of those who from any cause or other are contemplating emigaation. The farmers in Canada have had excellent crops during the last two years, and the industry is in a flourishing condition. The same thing may be said of other trades and callings, and reliable information upon all those matters may be obtained on personal applica- tion, or by letter to Mr. John Dyke, the Canadian Gov- ernment agent, Liverpool, who has just returned from a three months tour through Ontario, Manitober, and the North West Territories (Assiniboia, Alberta, Sas- katchewan, and Athabasca), and will give enquirers the benefit of his recent personal observation.
