THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 26. 1892. FOOTBALL. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE AT WARRING-I THE SHIP CANAL. TON. MR. J. PRICE'S TEST CASE. At the Borough Police Court, on Tuesday morn- ing,betore Messrs. Garnett (in the chair) and Cittest, John Price, who was formerly president of the Warrington Trades and Labour Couacil, and who lives in Winwick-et. was summoned for neglecting to send his son Thomas to school on the 14th November and at other times during the previous six months. Defendant :I am guilty of not. send- ing the lad to school. Mr. Riley: This is a case from Wycliffe School, and was dealt with by the committee last Thursday. The defendant's son had only passed the third standard. He is not free to leave school until he has turned 13 and has passed the fourth standard. Defendant had no objection- to send the lad to scheol. He was fully prepared to carry out the law, but he questioned Mr. Riley's right to bring him before the magistrates under the present summons, which said as plainly as he could read Eng- lish that a child must be sent to school, not before five and not ow 13.—Tie Clerk ruled that the summons was bad.—The Chairman (to defendamt).—Technically you are right, but the boy is bound to go to school. Defendant.—There is another thing that is misleading. The notices in the park say that all children must at- tend school from five to 13.—The Chairman : Yes.— Defendant : If that notice is not misleading I don't know what misleading is. If it had saia from five to 14 I could have understood it. The Chairman.—But there are conditions when children can leave at 13. Defendant: Yes, three sons of mine left at 13 at a Man- chester Board School. / keep my son away on principle. This is a matter of persecution. There are hundreds of poor working people in this town who are persecuted, and to whom an extra 4s. or ss. a week would be very handy during the winter months.—The Chairman : I don't see where the principle enmesh:v.—Defendant :The notice is misleading. The by-laws say from five to 13. —The defendant then began to read an extract from " Owen's Education Act, 1876, ' but, not being able to see very distinctly, handed the book to his son who stood at his side, and who read the following, in a very clear voice and in a manner which reflected great credit upon him :—" Direct Compulsion Bylaws. With re,,ard to bylaws, it will be remembered that by. the Education Act, 1870, School Boards were empowered, with the approval of the Education Department, to make bylaws for all or any of the following purposes : (1) Requiring the parents of children of such age not less than five years, or more than 13 years, as may be fixed by the bylaws (unless there is some reasonable excuse) to attend school.—The case was dismissed, after further discussion, upon the grounds that the summons was made out wrong.—Mr. Riley was told he could summon defendant under a new summons if he liked.
ACCIDENTS ON Tr-LE SEEP CANAL,

CORRESPONDENCE WITH THE BOARD OF TRADE. The following letter has Leen addressed by Mr. Whitw orth, the secretary of the Manchester Ship Canal, to the Assistant Secretary of the Railway Department, Board of Trade :

Manchester Ship Canal, Secretary's Offices, 41, Spring-gardens, Manchester, Nov. 18, 1892. Sir,—With further reference to your Ictter of the Ist inst., stating that you have received, through the Secretary of State for the Dome Department, a ern:- munication calling attention to the large number of accidents on public works during construction, in which it is stated that "an average of 12,00 ff men have been engaged in its construction (the Manchester Ship Canal), assisted by 500 locomotives and steam navvies, as well as an extensive list of ()tiler machinery. Time hospitals were built upon the works, with a large staff of surgeons and nurses in constant attendance, whose caergies were taxed to the ntrnost limit, during the whole time: The exact number of accidents, fatal and other- wise it is impossible to give. But from the reports of the inquests recorded in the local Press, I anr able to state the fatal'' cases with something near to accuracy, and the reports to our local secretaries give no good grounds for --ticulating minor cases. By this method of calculation, the fatal 'cases appear to be from 1,000 to 1,100; permanently injured, 1,300 ; partially injUred, 2,500. Those figures under rather dials over estimate the position," and requesting to be informed of the accuracy or otherwise of the figures quoted. I am directed to submit the following observations The average average number of men and boys employed upon the works from November 1887, to date is 10,500 per annum. The total number killed or who died from in- juries received on the works during the same period le- -130, an average of 26 per annum; permanently disabled, 165, an average of 33 per annum ; pa rtiafly injured, but not seriously, 997, an average of 199 per annum. The total number of accideats of all kinds, during the five years 1,292, or an average of 258 per annum. In most cases, the fatal accidents occurred through the men having been run over by locomotives or waggons ; two men and a boy were killt-d owing to a collision between two locomotives, and two men lost their lives by a train of waggons falling into a cutting 30ft.deep ; several fatal accidents occurred through falls from scaffolds and bridges and into cuttings. Many of the partial injuries are attributable to cleaning machinery whilst in motion, and to earth, Szc., falling from the buckets of the steam navvies, but in most of these cases the men were run over or crushed between waggons. There have been three hospitals on the works,aggre- gating sixty beds, the demands on which have never been excessive.

From the commencement until the 24th November, 1890, the works were carried out by the contractor, Mr. Thomas A. Walker and his executors, and since that date, partly by the company, and partly by other con- tractors.—l have the honour to be, sir, your obedient servant, (Signed) A. H. WHITWORTH, Secretary.

div.head: -*--- THE GLASGOW ATROCITY.
div.p: -*--- THE GLASGOW ATROCITY.
DECLARATION BY THE PRISONER.

The gardener William M`Ewan or Keown, who is in Custody charged with the murder of Mary O'Connor, whose horribly mutilated remains were found in West Lodge, Pollokshields, Glasgow, on the morning of the 13th October, was on Tuesday brought before Sheriff Birnie, and emitted a tleclaration. Since his capture— which was effected, it will be remembered, in the poli- cies of Sir John Stirling Maxwell, near the Half-Way Inn between Paisley and Glasgow, when he attempted to commit suicide by cutting his throat—Keown has been confined to the Royal Infirmary, where he has been carefully watched by a policeman dav and night. On Tuesday forenoon be was removed to the county build- ings in a cab, accompanied by two policemen and a sheriff's officer. The prisoner was dressed in a dark grey tweed suit belonging to himself, which was lound in West Lodge after the tragedy. Bound his throat, the wound on which is now almost completely healed, he had a bright blue bandage, and over it a large red muffler. No handcuffs were used. In the cab Keown conversed pleasantly about the weather, and expressed regret to those who accompanied him at having to appear before the sheriff in the black wide-awake head- gear and yellow cloth slippers with which he had been provided by the Infirmary authorities. From the cab to the cells,where he was confined for a few minutes be- fore he could be taken to emit his declaration, the pro- soner walked with a brisk step, and allowed no out- ward signs of concern, notwithstanding the gravity of the charge against him. During his confinement Keown has grown a short reddish beard, and has aged consider- ably in appearance. He is a man of about 34, but look- fully ten years older. During his stay in the Infirmary he has been seen by no one save his agent and tbe authorities. His removal on Tuesday was kept strictly private, and his arrival at the clunty buildings was witnessed by no one save a few officials. After making his declaration, Keown was removed in a cab to Duke- street prison, where he is now confined, charged with murder. The trial has been fixed to take place on the 27th December, at the Chrisimas sitting of the Circuit Court in Glasgow. The Crown authorities have resolved to take M'Neilly, the sailor who was in the house on the night of the tragedy, as a witness at the trial, instead of preferring a charge of complicity in the murder against him.

WALKER'S BREWERY 2ND V. BEDFORD Sr. JOSETH'S 2an.—This match was played at Leigh. The Brewery had the best of the game all through, and ran out winners by three tries seven minors to nil. BLINCORN raORNKTS V. WIDNES BOVERS.—ThiS match was played at Runcorn, in wretched weather, on Satur- day. After 55 minutes' play the visitors left the field, when the score stood, Hornets 1 goal 2 tries ; Widnes Rovers nil. Worthington, Si Ilington, and Cooper were the scorers for the Hornets, the first-named kicking a goal from the last try. RIINOORN RECREATION V. STOCKTON MUTH 2ND rlAM9).—These teams played at Runcorn on Saturday. In the first half the visitors seemed to overplay their epponents, but in the second half the game was more even, and eventually ended in a draw, the final score being—Stockton Heath, five minors ; Runcern Recrea- tion, three minors._

RUNCORN V. ST. HELENS.—ThiS match was played at Sc. Helens on Saturday, in wretched weather, rain fal- ling heavily throughout the game. The home team were strongly represented, whilst Runcorn had to sub- stitute the brothers Faulkner at three-quarter back in the place of Rodgers and Pendlebury, who are still unable to play through injuries. Runcorn :—Houghton, back ; Crompton, W. Faulkner, and J. Faulkner, three- quarters ; Abrams and Robinson, halves ; P. Riley, flampson, Farmer, Moores, Taylor, Williams, Davies, &vans, and Derbyshire. During the first half Runcorn pressed, and Crompton experiencel hard lines in not placing two goals from free kicks, the ball just going outside. The game was chiefly forward, owing to the heavy state of the ground. The second half was very keenly fought, and nothing but miners were scored, the game ending—Runcorn, three minors ; St Helens one minor. WARR/NOTON RANGERS V. WARRINGTON JUNIORS.—This League match was played on the Rangers' ground on Saturday,in wretched weather. The Juniors kicked off, ' Price returning to centre. From the first scrimmage formed, the Rangers rushed away and quickly notched a minor. Upon the drop-out the Juniors played up pluckily, but could not withstand the strong rushes of the home ferwards, who were playing a fine game. After , several repeated attacks Savage broke away, and opened the scoring account by securing a well-earned try,which was quickly followed with tries by R. Monks, Clarke, and 0. Warburton, goals being placed in two instances. The second half was all in favour of the home team, for whom Massey and Clarke added unimproved tries. The latter portion of the game was played in semi-darkness, but nothing further was recorded, and the Rangers retired victors by 2 goals, 4 tries' 4 minors, to Juniors nil. Referee, Mr. J. Boyle, W.F.C.

RUNCORN RICREATIO;I ;I. STOCKTON HEATH.—This match was played at Stockton Heath on Saturday. The Reereation team arrived early, but had to wait a long time before the home team all turned up. They placed a very strong team on the field, including several War- rington men. The home side kicked off in a heavy downpour of rain. A good return being made, play settled down in midfield. Nothing of importance took place, until Cross got hold, and putting in a good run gained a splendid try, the kick at goal failing. This roused the visitors, who now played up grandly, and gave the home men a lot of trouble, but were only rewarded with minor after minor, as the home full back intended playing a very safe game, and touched d)wn on every favourable occasion. A. Abel succeeded in getting over the line, but the 'Jail was ruled back, and the game ended in darkness, with the score : Stockton Heath, one try , Runcorn Recreation, eight minors. Ruiscorix RANGERS V. LATCHFORD RECS.—This match was played at Runcorn on Saturday afternoon in miserable weather. The following donned the jersey for the homesters :—Full back,C. H. Cook ; three-quarter backs. H. Hughes, J. Butterworth, and A. Houghton ; half-backs, E. Woodward,and .f. W. Johnson ; forwards, T. Woods, T. Goodier, W. E. Hough, J. Brennan, R. Miller, W. Faulkner, R. Harrison, W. Rushton, and A. France. The visitors, losing the toss, started the ball at 3.45, playing down field. Butterworth returned to ,1 Recs. 25, and, Johnson charging the visitors full backs, Butterworth got the ball on the bound and scored an easy try, his kick at goal being successful. Woodward and Faulkner were next prominent with the passing, the latter finally sending across to Hughes, who, failing to take it, missed a certain try. Woods got away with a fine dribble which almost ended in a score. Butter- worth getting hold from a scrimmage, ran well into the Recs.' 25, but failing to pass to Houghton, another easy try was lost. Half time score : Rangers, 1 goal ; Recs. nil. After the restart, the home forwards pressed, and Johnson getting hold, raced over at corner, but the try was disallowed. The hangers' forwards now rushed the Recs. on their line. Johnson again got over for the Rangers but the try was again disallowed. Some ' scrambling play ensued, Johnson at last crossing the I line successful,v, Butterworth failing at goal. Hough- ton attended to the drop out with interest, and Hughes getting hold from Butterworth ran over at corner, Cook failing at goal. Score, Rangers, 1-2-0 ; Recreation nil.

ASSOCIATION.

Sr. WIREURGH'S Y. EARLESTOWN WEST END.—This match took place on Saturday on the Roodee. It was raining when the teams faced each other, and for this reason only two thirties were played. The visitors were the first to prove dangerous, and tested Maguire with a stiff shot, but he was equal to the emergency, and clearel. The home left, then put in some good work, which resulted in the leather passing between the up- rights. This was disallowed, however, as off-side. The Saints, however, after twenty minutes' play, scored through Callaghan. Nothing further accrued before half-time. On re-starting the visitors' right got down and drew level. For a while the ball travelled freely from end to end with no result. However, Callaghan obtained possession, and passed to Coriam, who sent over to the right wing, and Jones put the finishing touch to a very pretty piece of passing. This also was awarded off-side. Nothing further rewarded either team's efforts, and the whistle blew with the score—St. Werburgh's, 1; Earlestown, 1.

RUNCORN V. NIIWTON-LB-WILLO WS.—This match Was played on Saturday, on the ground of the latter, under most unfavourable circumstances, the ground being sloppy, the rain constantly falling, and semi-darkness prevailing. Both teams played with ten men only, and turned out as follows :—Runcorn: Mainwaring goal- keepers ; Hughes and Blower, full-backs ; Bate, Richards and the Rev. Kingston, half backs ; Limb, A. Limb, Wright, and Antrobns, forwards Newton-le-Willows ; Floldgate, goalkeeper; Boarden and Dudgeon,full backs; Hammall and Whititt, half backs ; Pennington, Howard, Rogers, Heaton, and Naylor, forwards. Rogers kicked off for Newton, and after a short spell of play in mid- field, Antrobus came to the fore with some pretty drib- bling, and shot into goal, HcAdgate listing out. Wright meeting the return again shot in, Holdgate again clear- ing. The ball eventually went behind the line. Run- corn claimed a goal on the grounds that on both occa- ' sions Holdgate failed to clear before the ball was through the posts, but the point was not allowed. From the goal kick, however, the brothers Limb got hold, and I centreing to Wright, the last-named player neatly scored the first point for Runcorn. Both ends were now visited in turn, each custodian being required I to display his respective ability, when Rogers, making the best of an opportunity, drew level with a shot completely out of the reach of Mainwaring, who, as a rule, proves a great thorn in his opponents' side, rarely failing to clear when he has the ghost of a chance. Nothing further was scored at half time. On re-starting the ball was very difficult to see, and play, consequently, was of a very loose character. Limb, however, was conspicuous with a good sprint, and essaying a long quick shot, proved successful in giving his team the lead. Newton now pressed, and Hughes and Blower were called upon to defend, which they accomplished most efficiently. However, t'Ari home forwards were not to be denied, and from a scramble in front of goal, the ball was rushed through the posts, Runcorn claiming that it was only a corner, having never gone through the posts at all ; but the referee, after some doubt aml discussion, allowed the point. The game was now stopped, owing to the semi- darkness,with the lesult—Runcorn, two goals ; Newton- le-Willows, two goals.

div.head: MR. ASQUITH ON THE GOVERNMENT
div.p: MR. ASQUITH ON THE GOVERNMENT
P ROGRA.II ME.

Mr. Asquith, the Home Secretary, speaking in London, on Wednesday evening, said that so far as they had gone the Government had endeavoured to impress on the mind of the country that the administration of the great departments of the State would be conducted, not with a maudlin and sentimental disposition to give way to every cry and every clamour that was raised, but with an honest and resolute determination so far as the power of the law would allow to give the widest possible range and extension to the exercisa and enjoyment of popular rights. After declaring that Ireland was the first subject in the Government's programme, the right hon. gentle- man indicated the reforms in our electoral system and in local government which the Government had under consideration, and said that it would be found when Parliament assembled that they would present to the House of Commons legislative preposals which would satisfy the crying and long-delayed demands of the great mass of the:people of this country.

div.head: ISLE OF MAN MURDER. RESULT OF THE TRIAL.
div.p: THE ISLE OF MAN MURDER. RESULT OF THE TRIAL.

The trial of George Barker James Cooper, of West Clyne, Old Trafford, for the murder of his wife at Douglas was concluded on Monday amid great excite- ment. Sir W. Drinkwater, the first Deemster, a judge in his 81st year, summed up the evidence in this pro- tracted inquiry. His Honour's charge was throughout in favour of the prisoner, and says the " Manchester Guardian," our correspondent says that alter its delivery no other verdict than one of" manslaughter" appeared to he possible. The crime was committed lathe Regent Hotel, Douglas, on the morning of Satur- day the 3rd September. The prisoner and his wife arrived by the Fleetwood boat on the previous night, and Mrs. Cooper's face then bore the marks of severe blows. A barmaid asked the prisoner what he had been doing to his wife, and he replied that he had given her a good thrashing, and that he would " pay her out "—using one of the coarse expressions which were habitual with him. Next morning the couple were quarrelling in their bedroom, and a heavy fall was heard. After a considerable interval the prisoner was summoned by the manager of the hotel to open the door of the bedroom, which was found to be locked, and the persons who entered found Mrs. Cooper on the floor, quite dead, and with a deep and wide wound in the left breast. The prisoner said sho was "in a faint ;" then he said he "found her like that" on his return from the bank ; immediately afterwards he said it was "a sure case of suicide ; but after a considerable time had elapsed he put forward the defence that he had quarrelled with his wife, that she struck him on the face, and that in the heat of pas- sion he struck back, not knowing that he had a corn- knife in his hand. The wound bled profusely, but he thought it was not a serious one. He locked the door of the room and endeavoured to "bring her round." This was his last line of defence, and it was disclosed by or suggested to him very opportunely at the conclusion of the case which was brought forward by the Crown at the third preliminary inquiry. To prove that the de- ceased was a "violent, drunken woman," and one who would be likely to strike him when her temper was roused, evidence was given by several persons who are in the service of the prisoner or his father. It was also necessary to show that the prisoner had a peculiar habit nf holding nail-knives, and his statements on that head were supported by several witnesses. The cause of the quarrel which ended so fatally arose from the prisoner's relations with a woman, for- merly one of his employes, with whom he had lived in' America and this country, and whose husband had publicly horsewhipped him. It was on record also. that the prisoner had been tried ten years ago for at- tempting to shoot his first wife, and the nature., of the evidence on which he then obtained an acquittal is even yet fresh in the public mind. He had been repeatedly thrashed for assauting his unhappy wife. This was the, career with which the Deemster had to deal in laying.the case before the jury. He advised them to be cautious in accepting the prisoner's.version of the tragedy,. and remindectthem of the false statements he had made, but seemed to be of the opinion that the deceased was really a druniten woman. He suggested that the woman Rowles and the other servants had perhaps gone a little too far in their endeavour to save their master's son. His Honour at great length laid before the jury the whole of the sordid and miserable story, and reminded them, that the prisoner had practically pleaded guilty to the crime of manslaughter. The jury returned a verdict of man- slaughter, and the judges retired to consider their sen- tence. On their return into court Sir W. Drinkwater intimated that the judges did not disagree with thel " most merciful" verdict, and he sentenced the prisoner to penal servitude for ten years. The verdict and sem- tende.caused tremendous excitement in Douglas, and the crowd outside the court hooted the jurors most vigor- ously as they left the building. It was, in fact„ found necessary to employ the police for theirs protection,. and they were pursued with "howls of indignation." Cooper was "immensely relieved" by the verdict and sentence,

Trials for murder are, happily, very rare in the•blifrof Man. The last case before that of Cooper was that in which a man named Kelly was indicted for the murder of his wife. The couple had quarrelled, and Kelly took up a razor and nearly severed his wife's head from the ' body. This in the opinion of a Manx jury was merely manslau2hter—that is, they believed Kelly cat the woman's throat without any felonious intent. The man received the same sentence as that passed upon Cooper. In capital cases the jurors are selected in equab numbers from each electoral distriit of 'the island, and their names are announced in the press a week or two before the trial. They are thereby exposed to influences of all kinds.

div.head: JURYMMT- WELL TREATED.
div.p: THE JURYMMT- WELL TREATED.

One of the jurymen in the Cooper murder trial was interviewed on Tuesday. He was. warm in praises of the manner in which tse jury were" accommodated" at the hotel. The food and drink supplied were of the very best description, and it seems clear that the jurymen went into court every morning in a most benevolent frame of mind. It appears from admissions made by the juryman in the•course of the interview that eleven of the number were in favour of a verdict of mans slaughter before they retired to "consider %their ye,- diet, and the twelfth good-humouredly consented to waive his own prejudices for the sake of unanimity. Ile had thought far a time that Cooper really intended to injure his wile when he stabbed her in the heart, lard the other jurors were of a different opinion.

div.head: ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT ST. HELENS.
A SAD STATE OF AFFAIRS.

At St. Helens on Monday, before the Mayor (Mr. Arthur Sinclair) and other magistrates, Laura Cumberford, a young married woman, living in Parr Stocks-road, was charged with attempting to com- mit suicide. Chief Constable Wood stated that between four and five o'clock on Sunday afternoon prisoner jumped into what is known as the " Stinking Brook," near her own hcme. She had been married about eleven years, and had four children, but lived very uncomfortably with her husband. On Saturday night he badly assaulted her,, and gave her a black eye ; and on Sunday morning he again assaulted her. She said she would go and commit suicide, and he told her to go. She then went and jumped into the brook, but a man named John Jump went in and pulled her out. He (the Chief Constable) believed she had attempted to take herlifn before.—The Mayor asked If the husband was in court, and a working- man stood up. Chief Constable Wood: I believe he bru- tally illuses this poor woman, and further proceedings may be taken against him for it.—The Mayor spoke very kindly to the poor woman, and told her it was as much against the law to take her own life as to take anyone else's.—Mrs. Comberford : I have nothing to live for. My children have no pleasure, and I have not. I would rather die than be illused as I have been.— ale Mayor to the husband) : What have you to say P—The husband : On Saturday night the woman followed me out, and I would not let her come with me. She started screaming, and I threw my hand out and gave her a clout in the face, and pushed her against the wall. She went screaming and got other women out. —The Mayor: What are you ?—The Husband : I work at Wlcechnie's copper extracting works, and get 345. a week.—Mrs. Comberford said she would not live again with him.— Husband : I don't want to live separate, but I want her to keep to herself, and not to go to others —The Mayor : You must have assaulted her very badly for her to go and attempt to take her life.—Hus- band: Many a thing is done in a passion which we are sorry for afterwards.—The Mayor : Who gave her that black eye P—Husband : I gave it to her.—Mrs.Comber- ford : He has given me mails, a one before. I have no- where to go, but I will not live with him. When this is aver he will have revenge on me.—The Mayor : Would some of the neighbours take you for a few days ?• Ha will perhaps have more sense if you separate for a bit. —Husband: It she separates now, I will never live with her . any more.—The Mayor: You see that black eye. It is all very well to say that, when she has been driven (foolishly, no doubt) to try and take her life.—Ulti- mately, acting under advice, Mrs. Comberford took out a summons against her husband for assault. Mrs. Comberford promised not to make any more attempts upon her own life, and was discharged.

THE NORTHAMPTON MURDER. The trial of Andrew George Macrae on the charge of murdering Annie Pritchard in likely to take place sooner than was expected after the abrupt termination of the hearing at the Northampton Assizes last week. The juryman's departure from the court brought the pro- ceedings to a deadlock before the case for the prosecu- tion was completed, and Mr. Justice Kennedy, in the singular circumstances, adjourned the court and post- posed the trial to the next assizes. On Monday, however, he decided, with the consent of counsel and at the prisoner's wish, to return to Northampton after finishing the business at Warwick, and fixed December 20th as the most likely day for the trial.

div.head: EVICTED TENANTS COMMISSION
div.p: THE EVICTED TENANTS COMMISSION
ARCHBISHOP WALSFI GIVES EVIDENCE.

At the sitting of the Evicted Tenants Commission on Thursday Archbishop Walsh was examined in reference to the dispute en the Coolgreany estate. He stated that he had made careful investigation into the grievances of the tenants, and came to the conclusion that the claims they made were reasonable. He had, he said, made cal- culations as to the reductions in rent made in various parts of Ireland. The abatements at Coolgreany were small in comparison with those granted in many dis- tricts, and were quite inadequate. Asked what he would recommend by way of a settlement, the Arch- bishop said that essential points in any scheme would be the reinstatement of the evicted tenants. and the re- moval of the planters, the latter being compensated. With reference to eviction, he held that as there was dual ownership in the land, and the landlord and tenant were partners, it was not right that one of them should be in a position to proceed against the ether and consficate all his property. His view was that the landlord should recover debts due to him only by the same means which the tradesman had of doing so.

div.head: MANCHESTER ASSIZES. SINGULAR BREACH OF PROMISE CASE. ENORMOUS BETTING TRANSACTIONS.
div.p: MANCHESTER ASSIZES. SINGULAR BREACH OF PROMISE CASE. ENORMOUS BETTING TRANSACTIONS.

The business of the Manchester Winter Assizes was .opened on Wednesday; Mr. Justice Bruce presiding in the Crown and Mr. Justice Grantham in the Civil Court. In his charge to the Grand Jury Mt. Justice Bruce re- ferred to the large number of cases in the calendar which arose out of a disregard of the ordinary family relations. In these cases, and in others in which there was a general disregard of the decencies of life, they had an indication of corruption which was deep-seated and deplorable. In the Nisi Prius Court, before Mr. Justice Grantham, a remarkable action, for breach of promise was heard. The plaintiff was a widow living in Byde, where the defendant, a constable in the Cheshire Con- stabulary, passed as a single Than. After he be- came engaged to the plaintiff it transpired that he had been married for some years to a Miss Woolley, the occupier of a licensed house, but that the marriage had been kept secret because the defendant had married contrary to the police regur lations which obtain in Cheshire. The plaintiff said she had known both the defendant and his wife for a num- ber of years, but had not the slightest idea that they were married. The jury awarded the plaintiff SSO4 lii a case in which a publican at Borwich sought to recover a sum of money,the proceeds of a bet he had made with a man named Wilson,or Walker, who carried on his business on the continent, the Judge made some very strong'observations as to the prevalence of betting,. and the practice of it under the circumstances disclosed in the case. The defendant's counsel urged that his client conducted his transactions honourably, and stated that in the last few years he had paid away the extraordin- ary amount of £BOO,OOO in the pursuance of his avoca- tion. Upon a technical point judgment was &fen for the defendant.
WIDNES MUNICIPAL 81-ELECTIONS.

• In order to complete the constitmion of Widnes Town Council, eltetione, took place on Tuesday in five wards in the new orough. At the previous election on November lat„eighteen councillors were elected, live of whom were elevated teethe Alder- maniebench, namely Aldbrsnen TiMMiN William- son, Tilley, Sadler, and Wareing, andvacancies were thus created in West &ilk, Waterloo;yictoria, Simms Cross, and Halton Wards. There was a contest in each of these wards. In West Bank ward, Mr. Win. Winwood Goinage,"eldest san of the mayor,. was opposed by Mr. J hehuallid wooch estate agent, who was for 19 years mu/ember of the Local Board, and only ceased his connection when that body came to an end. Mr. Gossage. had also, made .an acquaintance with public work, having 'held a seat on the late Board for three years. Both gentlemen came forward independent of politics! In Waterloo Ward, there were three aspirants for the vacant seat, Messrs. Charles Hemingway-, builder, and Mr. J. C. Crawford, schoolmaster, seeking election.. as I independent, and Mr. John Gough, powder packer, as a representative of labour. Attempts wore made by the friends of the independents to effect a compromise by which one could "gracefully " retiie, but terms could not be arranged, and both went to the poll, and the sequel Is shown in the result. The contest in Victoria Ward aroused much interest from the fact that Mr. 13:- Brown, a gentleman who has rendered valuable services. to the town on the Local Board, was opposing the.i Catholic nominee, Mr. J. Fitzpatrick,. in what is truly described as a Catholic stronghold. Mr. Hugh O'Donnelf,an ex-inspector of the Cheshire poliee,had been nominated as a National candidate, but he retired before the day of polling arrived. In Simms' Cross, Ward two Independents were opposed in the person of Mr. G. Davies, coal merchant, and Mr. J. W. Knowlewsolicitor, and as it' was an open secret that the latter, would receive the Catholic vote, his prospects of success rere consideredvery bright. Both candidates worked hard. Again in Halton ward the struggle lay between candi- dates who came forward, independent of politics; viz., Mr. F. NeWand Mr. D. Wright. In each ward the can- didates were supplied with numerous helpers and con- veyances, and although there was no appearance of excitement the polling went on steadily throughout the day, and the percentage of burgesses who polled was very largo:. _ . .

'lieltTayor, Alderman Gossage, LP., with the assist- ance of the Town Clerk (Mr. Oppenheim), and the deputy (Mr. &elk) had made arrangements for taking the poll on as complete a scale as possible. In Halton Ward there were two polling stations in Warrington-road schools, the presiding officers being Messrs. C. El. Lewis and J. The following was from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m., and at the latter hour, the ballot boxes were conveyed to the Town Flall,where the counting took place under the supervision of the Mayer, the followingre aldermen acting as returning officers for the wards named :—.Balton, Alderman Williamson; Simms Cross, Alderman Sadler ;Victoria, Alderman Tilley; Waterloo, the Mayor ; West Bank, Alderman Timmis. The count- ing was carried out by the presiding officers and their clerks, and the counting agents appointed by the candi- dates teem Councillors .Elullough and Christie for Mr. Neil ; Mr. J. Randle for Mr. Wright ; Mr. F. Lawrinson for Mr. Davies.; Councillor G. I. Neil for Mr. Knowles ; Mr. T. Atherton for Mr. Brown; Mr. P. J. Rowe for Mr. Fitzpatrick ;:Mr. D. J. By half-past eight a large crowd load assembled in front of the Town Hall to await the result, and at 9204 when the Mayor declared the figures from the balcony, there many hundreds present, and the utmost enthusiasm was manifested. div.head: RE-VACCINATION.
div.p: RE-VACCINATION.

Sic—My letter has brought me a communication from the Anti-vaccination society- The skill with which statistics are managed by this society so as to prove anything reqnired is wonderful. I will give only one instamee out cf many. It is stated " that in the Sheffi- eld epidemic 243 died who were confessedly vaccinated" It is well known that vaccination does not confer life- long immunity, and when the other part of the report is examined, it will be found that out of 56,233 persons re-vaccinated during isam two only were doubtfully attacked and none died. If the writer of the leaflets, which are-offered for sale at a very profitable rate, had published the whole report, and all the facts, as any unbiased person would have &tie, the matter would have a very different appearance. I have personally a very strong objection to vaccina- tion, but tins has not prevented my submitting to it at three different periods, not only for my own gaiety, but also for the safety of those about me. In the face of the statements published the caution of the writer against any statistics except hie .own, is exceedingly cool. The report ef the German Government on re-vaccination published in the London" Standard "of November 15th should be cnite sufficient to demolish this seller of leaf- lets and terrifier of silly women.—Yours &c. THOMAS FLETCHER.

div.head: EPIDEMIC.
div.p: THE EPIDEMIC.

Sir,—! shaE.esteem it a favour if some of your numer- ous readers will kindly give a satisfactory reply to the following queries :—As we are told the prevailing epi, demic is strongly contagious, can it be conveyed from one family to auther, in the dress which is worn, and so transmitted to those congregated at public meetings? We., as heads of families, are advised not to attend pub- lic meetings, whilet our children are compelled to attend theyublic day schools, where they may possibly be seated by the side of another child from an infected home. It is a fact tLat such has been the case, and I now ask wherein lies the consistency of the authorities? Why should not we be able Co rusticate or isolate our children during the epidemic, without a visit from the School Attendance Officer, who is in- structed to enforce the attendance ? Lastly, I would ask whv the authorities at Lymm order the closing of the public schools, while here it is not deemed advisable to do so ? A thriving borough like Warrington should be the forerunner in matters of this kind. The news- papers report that the new hospital could not be placed at Pear Tree Farm, because of two schools being about a mile from the site, but hers we have 4 very large schools in close proximity to Hope Hospital, and nnmer- Ails parents, &c., have been seized with the disease, , who have or had children attending school. By insert- ing the above you will greatly oblige.—Yours respeat- fully: Novembyr 23rd, 1892.
a N. B.
THE SMALLPDX OUTBREAKB..

Sir.—The recent outbreaks of smallpox at Warrington and elsewhere affords an excellent opportunity—which is being fully taken advantage of—to proclaim the sup- posed virtues of re-vaccination. Simple primary vac- cination, which, according to the dead Jenner and the living Simon, would render every recipient of it abso- tuely secure from an attack of the disease, is now, per- force, given up by the Medial picffssio7 'Ft; kir. tell us, however, that it mitlgateS ari attack ; but as no human being can tell lelP lightly or severely any one might be attacke3, this assurance is rather a proof of the confidence than of the logic of such comforters. I note in a recent newspaper report that Dr. Adams, the Medical Officer for Runcorn,has been saying that at Warrington "Nothing remained but re-vaccination," "and," he added, "but they had no compulsory powers of enforcing this." He might have gone on and said, "nor will they ever have such powers." At the same time he rather sapiently remarked, that by the acquies- cence of the Ship Canal authorities " in his directions" there would be no one under his control not re-vacci- nated within 48 hours within the immediate circle of' inspection. One is rather curious to learn by what gal authority these "authorities" or any other, pres•umeor pretend to enforce re-vaccination on adults P. There is something naive, almost funny, in some 09„ the reported remarks of Dr. Adams. He says, .In.had found at the Ship Canal huts six or seven grown up children who had not been vaccinated at all ' 110 w shocking! The im- plication is pretty plain that these children are focuses of disease. If Dr. Adams will search the records for Irian's, years post of only nee smallpox hospital, he will finclibat at Highgate, London, from over 80 per cent, up to, in recent years, 94 per cent, of thg patients there were officially certified as being vaccinated. If he will refer to the army report for 1889, he will find that our rigidly vaccinated troops in Egypt that year died from smallpox at the rate of 1.750 per million, while in that year England, with its millions of unvaccinated persons and young children, suffered a smallpox mortality rate of only one per million. Just now attempts are being made to descry Leicester's signal success in dealing with smallpox and similar diseases solely by means of notifi- catioa and isolation. These attempts are very ill- founded, as I hear from a sure source that Leicester is overcoming rapidly her present difficulties. Most probably the mischief at the Ship Canal Works is due to the aggregation of masses of men under insani- tary coaditions, and with no proper hygienic super- vision. It is all very well to order the nuisance inspec- tors to freely supply disinfectants at the Ship Cane huts; but this is but a tinkering at the business if the huts are overcrowded, unhealthy, and there is no prompt and effective system of isolation. The question of build. lag an infectious diseases hospital at a cost of £1,200 has been referred by the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Autho- rity to a Committee. Perhaps in a few years such a place may be erected to meet a contingency like the present one. In the meantime, however, a very good substitute for such a hospital may be found in the use of canvas tents, and it is to be hoped that some means of the kind may be rapidly improvised in all places which are situated as is just now Warrington. 'Phis will be a thousand times better than placarding the district in praise of the imaginary virtues ot vaccination. Some high authorities very much deprecate vaccinating and revaccinating during a smallpox epidemic ; but this course usually commends itself to the average medical mind. It is, at any rate," good business" in a com- mercial sense as one medical man has been known to pocket £6O a week from vaccination fees during a small- pox scare. Hence one very solid reason why the dealers in this mythical and mystical stuff (vaccine) are always so ready to chant its praises. Considering what is now known of the true inwardness of this vaccination business —thanks to investigators such as Professor Crookshank., Dr. Creighton, and Mr. Alfred Russell Wallace, among others, it is to be hoped that the press will not back up the outcry of medical men for more vaccination. Its protection is very problematical, and it most certainly has its own inherent and unavoidable evils and dangers. If the local authorities of any place need guidance from long and painful experience they would do well to consult their brethren at Leicester ; and they would thus learn a far more excellent (and also cheaper) way of combating smallpox than by polluting the blood of their people with the so-called vaccine. At present it is very much a case of the blind and pedantic medical officers leading the blind and simple members of local boards, &c. ; and the result is what miglip be anticipated.— Yourstke.,, 22 Nov., 1892.
J. F!.
"LEGAL EIGHT HOURS FOR MINERS."

Sir,—" Cymro," from his first to his last letter, has stated so much at my expense, concerning himself, and what he has done for miners, /sc., that justice has ren- dered it essential for me to test him. It has been pain- ful to me to have to follow " Cymro " on these lines. He commenced it. I could not, without being cowardly, do less than defend my position. But I hope in future

not to need to follow hi zn. on such lines. I will simply meet "Cyrnro'e argr ,ments on their merits. He has only stated the old a, murnents against legal shortening of working hours- -what Mr. John Bright, &c., did against the Ten P Bill. Time has proved that all „mire such arguments give Mr. Bright, Sze., the lie. It is es- sential for "Cy, mro" to disprove, if he can, historical 0 facts before I- A caa make , good his position. (1) I have proved that /mid enactments for shortening workia.• hours did n A ruin the trade, wages, er commerce of the empire th,,r4. *f Cyeiro "cannot refute these facts. .(2) Workme a or workwomen, cannot do as good work when r eayncl—er r 4 unhealthy by overwork—too long 'hours per d as otherwise they could do. (3) The working- class, are rendered incapable of that mental and moral Im'drovement and development that otherwise they r.. 111161 attain to were their health not destroyed by work- ing too long and too hard. (4) Health laws, which are the essential bases of all true progress cannot be studied and followed as they should be, by the over- worked masses of the empire. (5) It follows therefore that shortening of working hours for all kinds of work which renders the workers dull of mind, and unhealthy in body, ought, in the highest and best interest, of the empire, to be as speedily as circumstances will possibly allow, made hard and fast by law. (8) Legal shorten- ing, &c., of working hours would, especially for miners, prevent much idleness in the beginning of each week, and., further still, do much to prevent accidents in mines. (7) Legal eight hours would tend to produce more order, better system, and good feeling among all sections of masters, as well as as among employes. (8) It would be the most effectual remedy against the ' sweating of needlewomen ; and all classes, at present groaning and:starving. in this country; while their heart- less, and godless employers are growing fat."—Faith- fully yours, - -- - - ---
R. STOREY.
180, Orford-lane, Warrington. Nov. /8, 1892.

div.head: JOHN CROSTIELR.
div.p: JOHN CROSTIELR.
THE SAGE OF PENKETH AND HIS SHILLELAGH..

Six,—Not for one moment do I call in question the Sage of Penketh's statement, so oracularly put forth in his postscript, " with other than 'reasoning beings, literary, or other, I have equally effective methods." This is the characteristic and leading feature of the manner in which Mr. Peer's conducts an argument. In all his writings there is a conspicuous absence of reason- ing, and, in its place, there is substituted the formid- able weapon known as the shillelah. A short time ago the Sage of Penketh was seen rushing into the battle field, and, brandishing aloft his shillelah, threatening the cranium of an innocent " goose." Now, he is seen flourishing the same ‘deadly weapon over the head of no less important a personage than Dr. Mouncey. It is curious to find the Sage of Penketh place so much faith in this weapon.. In ancient days, the Sage was wont to use an enchanted wand; and by means of that weapon, communicated with the world of spirits, and summoned their occupants at will. Whether the Sage of Penketh can perform the same feat with his shillelagh remains to be seen. As a leading agnostic„ ime would be inclined to think he bid farewell to the world of spirits; but his spasmodic and convulsive invocation of the shades isf Watt, Mill, and Whately, would lead one to suppose that the instinc.; of immortality is still powerful in the breast of the Sage of Penketh. It is well-known that, on the other side the cha,nnel, the shillelagh is chiefly used for the purpose of splitting open refractory craniums ; but Mr. Peers will probably ficd it more useful in despatching a " cockroach "when it "intrudes "into his garden or his night cap. Mr. Peers again refers to my statement regarding the destruction of the weak; and, by doing so, he evidently thinks he has scored. He writes as follows :—" The Agnostic does not takeupon himself to judge as to who is, and to who is not, so fitted (for life) ; he is content to leave our common mother to do that, and she does it very effectually. It is the natural savage man who thus assumes nature's prerogative; when he rises to become an Agncstic and an Evolutionist he ceases to do this or anything so immoral." Now, Mr. Peers admits that the laws of nature are necessary and immutable, and there- fore cannot be broken. All phenomena are capable of reduction to saturat laws; and, consequently, all know- ledge is confined to them. They are the seat and home of all truth and reality. On discovering these phenomena and their laws, it is necessary for man to accomodate himself to them, and to his surroundings. Now, accord- ing to Mr. Peers, this is the function which the savage performs when he "assumes nature's prerogative," and destroys the weak and dying and, conversely, the cul- tured man of the 19th century must fail to do so when he refrains from doing so. Mr. Peers must also not for- get that behind nature there is "the Power, not our- selves, that makes for righteousness." If it be "im- moral "for the cultured man to put the weak and dying to death, it must be equally so for the "Power that makes for righteousness" to do so, i.e., this Power mus: become immoral or unrighteous. Accordingly, Mr. reerst by referring to this agurrient, seems to me to have I made the weakest exhibition of himself yet known. Finally, the answer which Mr. Peers makes to my statement, that his conclusions in one department of science must not conflict with those of another, or with the great law of the conservation of energy, is charac- teristic of the man, and clearly shows how dexterously Mr. Peers is able to wield his beloved shillelagh in prefer- ence to solid argument. "This" he says "completely ' flabbergasts ' me Does the Sage of Penlvtth imply byr this s-tatement that whatever branch o knowledge or of special science "flabbergasts" him contains a contra- diction, and is unworthy ot study ? If so, it requires neither a prophet nor the son of a prophet to declare that his pluck is far ahead of his science. In such an absence of all reasoning and of anything bearing the slightest pretence to argament,,ii; !,r; no wonder that Mr. Peers falls back upon his only e. aa.Zan. shillelagh.—Yours, &c,

div.head: MONSTER VINEG AR VAT:
div.p: A MONSTER VINEG AR VAT:

The Lancashire Vinegar Company, Radcliffe, have re- cently had lxed for them by Messrs. Henry Roberts and Co., Mile End-road, London, one of three large vats for the storage of malt vinegar. In circumference it is 50/ feet ; at the base the diameter is le feet, and at the head 14 feet 5 inches ; the staves are le feet si inches in length, and iron hoopes which encircle it, measure 940 feet. It is made of English oak, and the weight of timber is about five tons. The storage capacitr is 20,000 gallons., which will weigh nearly 90 tons. It is the largest vat for the storage of of vinegar in Lanca- shire. A few days ago a party was held in it, the accommodation being sufficient for 24 persons.

div.head: ••• A LABOURER BEATEN TO DEATH.
div.p: ••• A LABOURER BEATEN TO DEATH.
CHARGE AGAINST SOLDIERS.

At Warwick on Tuesday the two uldiers, Welsh and King, arrested on Saturday night for the murder of Jas. Russell, whom they flogged to death with buckled belts, were brought before the magistrates and remanded for a week. The attack, according to the statsment of lE.. spector flail, was premeditated. In the afternoon the soldiers were drinking at an inn, and one of them used offensive language to the barmaid. Russell, the bar- maid's brother, strongly protested, and Welsh, angry at the man's interference, challenged him to fight. Russell declined the encounter, but at night, on returning home, was waylaid by the soldiers, and they beat him till he fell and died.

mAt the usual meeting of "unemployed " on Tower Hill, on Wednesday, statements were made to the effect that " the unemployed were in possession of arms which they had been trained to use." Inquiry shows that this threatening report has reference to the fact that some of the men are rifle volunteers, and, in defiauce of orders to send in their arms in common with other men, have retained the weapons in their possession.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER. 26, 1892
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER. 26, 1892
WARRISGTON COUNTY FOOTBALLERS.
THE NEW FULL-BACK INTERVIEWED.

If the Warrington football team, as a whole, have been latterly prevented front making any brilliant exhibitions, some of their individual members have been more fortunate. Upon two of them Dame Fort une has smiled her sunniest smile. They are Joe Boscow,now the indomitable County full- back, and J. Jolley, one of the forwards of the 1 same celebrated team. The Tact, of both being chosen to play against Cumberland on Saturday, and again in the greatest of the inter-county matches—Lancashire v. Yorkshire—which takes place to-day, is an honour in regard to which local foo-Lballers can afford to boast the figurative "feather in their caps." Jolley as an active and able forward, is a familiar figure in Warrington football circles, and his ;election by the County has not created much surprise. The fine fashion in which he conducted himself on Saturday, whilst astonishing many who did not know him was but the ordinary standard of his high class play. But, as regards Boscow, public attention was close, and interest keen, when he made his debut at Whalley Range. And he certainly, in his responsible work as full-back, constituted him- self the hero of the day. It was after the match on Saturday that our in- terviewer went in search of the brilliant full-back. It struck him that he ought to glean something of the period in Joseph's life when his sporting ideas were passing through that interesting ordeal of be- ing taught how to shoot. There is no doubt he learned how to shoot—at goal, and well, too. Presently Mr. Boscow was discovered in possession of a county jersey, with the collar torn off, and the beautiful red rose badge hanging by two threads.

"That is a somewhat graphic indication of your performance," said the interviewer, pointing to the jersey. "Yes, it gives a little indication of the way in which one's toilet is disarranged in the game oi foot- ball." _ _ .

There didn't seem to be much hope of obtaining any personal information from Joe. He appeared to be more inclined to speak upon some one else's good points rather than his own. But it wasn't iong before the interviewer, in the course of his search, discovered some one who knew the full-back almost as well as he knows himself. He was the captain of the first football club in which Joseph played. " Mr. Boscow," said their friend," was born in Church-st., Warrington, March 16th, 1869, and in 1886 he commenced his football career by joining St. James's Rovers as full back. He stayed with the club one year, after which he transferred his services to the La chford True Blues, better known as the " Square Table," in which team he served for a period of two years. A medal competition was insti- tuted (open to all the junior organisations) by the Premier Town club, the Warrington P.C., and it was in this competition that Boscow made his mark. It was through his instrumentality that the "True Blues" in the second year of the competition won the silver medals;, and the Warrington F. C. noting this playeis sterling work ultimately persuaded him to join their ranks. After this step his success became assured, as he gained many encomiums by his superior and gentlemanly play. He was ultimately called upon in 1888, to fill the full back position in the first team, which he has done since, in a manner highly creditable to so young a player. I can say unhesitatingly that a more unassuming player it is impossible to meet with. "I have known him constantly since he first commenced football, and I know that wherever he has gone as a footballer, there be has soon made himself a favourite. It is only his fine consistent good play that has now gained him the distinction, which he has so long merited, that is the place of Fall Back for the Lancashire County. And his debut in that team, under such exceptional circumstances, was undoubtedly a remarkable one, and one which may ultimately call him to fill a more prominent position. He is thoroughly deserving of success, and 1, like all who have made his acquaintance, heartily wish him success. " There is another matter respecting his general ability as an all round athlete. Ile is a fair bicycle rider, a good cricketer, and an. active member of the "Gym."

been drawn against the Dolobran Athletic Club, Birmingham, for the first round. The contest, which will probably be a tough one, is likely to come off at Birmingham, as the Dolobran men have the chcice of " ground." They till naturally elect to play at home. Well, perhaps if they do it will not be much to the de- triment of the Warrington "eight." They somehow appear to be of a modest disposition, for last year when they contested with Exeter at home, and before their friends, they were not quite up to the scratch, Exeter Hall meet the Liverpool Gymnasium as their first , opponents.

The eight selected, we believe, are the same as last year. One or two of them the public will be glad to see, for last season they were showing signs of increas- ing improvement. Motram and Podmore for instance were commencing to shine.

The other week we made a suggestion to the Corn, of the " Gym," that the fortnightly entertainments given last year should be revived. The Committee intend to do this directly the epidemic has subsided. We do not know, however, whether they will act upon the other part of our suggestion, and engage, in the musical por- tion of the entertainments, local at tistes.

div.head: • – PE NKETH.
div.p: • - PE NKETH.
ACCIDICNT.

On Monday an accident occurred to Mr. Bardsley, of Yew Tree Farm. It seems that he was in the act of getting into a one-horse cart, when some part of the gear suddenly broke, causing the cart to upset. Mr. Bardsley was precipitated to the ground, the cart falling upon him, snapping one of his legs in two places. Medical aid was at once procured. Ile is progressing favourably.

div.head: WEDDING.
div.p: WEDDING.

On Tuesday afternoon a marriage took place at the Wesleyan chapel, the contracting parties being Miss Alice Maud Seed Wolstencroft, and Mr. John Midwood, of Widnes. Mr. Thomas Seed gave the bride away, while her brother acted as best man. The Rev. T. Ross, of Warrington, performed the ceremony. The bridesmaid was Miss E. Wolsten- croft. The scholars of the school where Miss Wolstencroft has been a teacher lined the road and loudly cheered the happy pair. The wedding pre- sents were numerous. The couple proceeded to Blackpool to spend their honeymoon.

div.head: SMALLPDX EPIDEMIC
div.p: THE SMALLPDX EPIDEMIC
AT WARRINGTON.

CONTINUED ABATEMENT. We are glad to be able to announce that the decrease in the number of cases has continued all week. Up to Wednesday last eight cases were notified from the previous Friday. Wednesday and Thursday no cases were reported, but yester- day five or six came under the notice of the authorities.
THE CLOSING OF THE SCHOOLS. The following letter, it will be seen,has reference to the proposal that has been made that the schools should be closed :

Health Department, Town Hall, Warrington, 24th Nov., 1892. Dear Mr. Town Clerk,—ln reference to the letter addressed to the Mayor by the Rector " Re the closing of schools." I give the hllowing opinion. The view taken is that more is done to prevent the spread of the epidemic by the means at present employed, viz. the exclusion of scholars known to come from infected houses, than would be the case were the schools to be closed, which would really mean an increase of facilities of inter-communication between children of different households, and would entaii the giving up of that con- trol which the Sanitary Authorities are at present able to exert by the means above referred to. The closing of schools has been known under similar circumstances of r ours to result in a spread of infection, and the compara- tive rarity of smallpex among the children at present is certainly indicative that the congregation of them in schools has not been an important means of spreading the disease. Unvaccinated children would certainly I have been expected to have taken it, and, though a considerable portion of them have been found in the schools, smallpox has been infrequent among them. —I am, yours sincerely, JOHN H. GORNALL, Medical Officer of Health.

VACCINATION STATIONS. Each evaning during the week local medical men, have attended, and will continue to attend the follow- ing stations for the purpose of vaccination : the Work- men's club, John-st., the office of the School Attendance fficer, Bank Park ; the Christ Church schools, Wash-lane Latchford ; and the Workingmen's Mission, Bank Quay. , The following gentlemen are in charge of the various places, namely, Drs. Gornall, Braide,Bowden, Peacocke, Ronald, and Reginald Smith. The Board of Guardians have issued notices to the effect that the Medical Officer will attend at the Golborne-st., Baptist sehoolroom every Tuesday evening from seven to eight o'clock, and at his office at the Town Hall every Friday afternoon at two o'clock for the purposes of vaccination, until fur- ther erders. During the week there have been about 1,600 persons re-vaccinated at these stations.

EFFECTS ON WORKETOPLE. On Tuesday night 172 men, women, and children ' passed under the hands of Dr. Peacock at the Club House, John-street. Gat of the 450 workmen employed at Messrs. Rylands Bros. wireworks, about one-third have been vaccinated. The reason of 'the number being BO small is found in the fact that the port,on of the town in which the works are situated, has almost entirely escaped the infection. The only cases of small- pox among the employes are those of a man and a boy. Of the number vaccinated something like a dozen are at present unable to follow their employment. At Cockhedge Mills 1,100 persons have been vaccinated, and the majority of the workrnea at Bewsey and Dallam Forges have undergone similar treatment. A large number of persons engazed at these places are tem- porarily disabled from work.

div.head: TWO CONCERTS ABANDONED.
div.p: TWO CONCERTS ABANDONED.

Mr. W. E. Atkin, hon. secretary of the Warrington Musical Society, as will be seen from an advertisement in another column, intimates that en accoant of the prevailing epidemic, and the consequent refusal of the irineipal vocalists to vihit the town, the committee is reluctantly compelled to abandon both the concerts Fxed for next Friday evening, November 25th, and December 22nd. "DARKEST ENGLANDERS" FRIGHTENED.

A meeting in connection with the "-b-aa-e-s-lin-gland scheme " had also been arranged for, but it has been postponed owing to the outbreak of smallpox, It should have been held in the Co-operative Hall, on Monday next, but we are informed that " General Booth and his friends will bring the matter before the townspeople later on."

div.head: TRADESMEN APPEAL.
div.p: TRADESMEN APPEAL.

During the week a written appeal, signed by a large majority of the tradesmen of Warrington,was forwarded to the Mayor and officials of the borough,asking for protec- tion "against the detrimental statements made by Dr. Fox Lyrnm." The statements alluded to refer to those issued by Dr. Fox, warning country people against hav- ing anything whatever to do with either persons or things from Warrington. This is said to have affected trade in town to anjalmost ruinous extent. We believe that the Mayor, assisted by his colleagues, has con- sidered the matter and decided upon issuing a kind of "counterblast" to Dr. Fox's placards. THE DISEASE AT LYIESI.

The epidemic of smallpox in Lymm shows no signs of increasing. The persons infected with the disease all reside in the neighbourhood surrounding the house where the first case occurred. It is said that the cause of the outbreak was due to a woman visiting her son in Warrington who was stricken down by the disease. The schools were closed last week for an indefinite period, and a concert which was announced to be held in the Drill Hall on Monday night was abandoned,owing to the prevailinZ epidemie, The legal. uthori ties are exeicising the greatest precautions in the matter, arid it is very probable that the scourge will soon die cut.

div.head: ANOTHER CASE AT NEWTON.
div.p: ANOTHER CASE AT NEWTON.

A fresh case of smallpox has occurred at Newton, the unfortunate victim being a gentleman well known in that village. The case has been completely isolated, and the gentleman's family has been removed from the house. Dr. Handyside has charge of the case, and under his care the patient is progressing, favourably. The gentleman in question, and the victim of the case which occurred last week, are both employed at Messrs. McCorquodale and Co.'s works, Newton, and as a matter of precaution, the firm has recommended the re-vaccination of their office staff, a suggestion which has been readily complied with. In additionk to this the various medical men are having rather a busy time at preSent, as a large number of the residents pfboth Earlestown and Newton kave undergone re-vaccination. It is pleasing to note, however, that not a single casks of smallpox has occurred at Earlestown. Since writing the above a case has occurred in Legh- st., Earlestown. The patient in this instance is the sister of a man who died at Warrington about a fort- night ago from ths disease, and whom she, nursed through his illness. She has been unwell for A few days ' back and has been attended by Dr. Handyside, who on Wednesday discovered that she was suffering from smallpox, and on the case being duly reported, she was removed on Thursday to the house in Warrington,where her brother died. Her husband accompanied her to Warrington. The case is only of a mild form, but this is accounted for by the fact that the patient was reva c- cinated about a fortnight ago.

div.head: HAYDOCK.
div.p: HAYDOCK.

Another case, making the third, has occurred at Hay- dock, the victim being a girl 10 years of age, living in Lyme-st. She has been removed to the temporary hospital, on Newton Common, and is under the care of Dr. Hayward,

div.head: ROUT THE EPIDEMIC.
div.p: A ROUT THE EPIDEMIC.
BY A CORRESPONDENT.

At length the panic and turmoil is quieting. The storm is gradually abating, and the tumultous sea of public apprehension is resuming' its calm surface. A reassuring abatement of thel smallpox,in Warrington,has continued all the week.l But the course of the foul disease demon has left in its wake many things. It has left vacant places in 26 homes, from where it bore its doomed victims; and it has left grief and sorrow in the hearts of those who have lost their offspring,and in the hearts of offsprings who have lost parents. It has caused pain and suffering, and dread to 500 stricken p.ople; and thrust into many homes poverty and want, It has half-ruined many of our tradesmoa, and last, but not least—it has taught to those res- ponsible for the health of the town a lesson, which it is to be hoped, thy, and all who have learned it, will never forget. To dwell upon the laxity or the shortcomings of any individuals a the Town Council would be superfluous. But a word of warning to the whole body would perhaps be timely. There is an old saw which says " Ntver put off till to-morrow what you can do to-day." Had the Town Council of this town heeded the simple injunction of that jewel of wis- dom, years ago, perhaps all the suffering, and anguish, and confusion, and expense, Which has , been inflicted upon the people of Warrington, would have been averted. What, for instance, has become of the slum property—which have been described as the "Black spots of Warrington ?" Those hovels and areas were condemned by Dr. Gornall, as hot-beds of disease, vet they exist still as a monument of reproach to the Town Council of Warrington. Then again, what has been done with the drains, which the authorities have known for years were in a condition calculated to create and propagate disease and even death ? It is said that all the drains which empty themselves into the river, are so unhappily constructed as to form one of the most dreaded and vital dis- crepancies in the whole of our scheme of sanita- tion—or insanitation. a be outputs of these drains are but a few inches above the low-tide mark of the river. Consequently every tide floods them and

washes back the drainage to the sewers, where is created that obnoxious and poisonous stench which often permeates our streets. In the times of wet weather like the past few weeks the river is swollen so as to keep the drains con- stantly flooded, and person%living in certain parts of Bold-st. and neighbourgbod, W ilderspool-road, and other places, are kept constantly aware of this by a stpnch which even, in some cases, finds its way to the bedrooms. surely it may be insisted that the authorities shoul.i recognise the necessity of removing the dangers of bad sanitation which I have named.

During the whole of last week hundreds of us swarmed tivon our medical men fir the purpose of being vaccinated or re-vaccinated, and hundreds of fretful minds were calmed when the calf's lymph had been inoculated. On every hand one met with the query " Have you been vaccinated ?" And so many answered in the affirmative by pointing •A 3 the limp-hanging arms, as to remove any danger of inaccuracy in saying that more than three parts of the inhabitants of Warrington had undergone the operation. Indeed, so common is it amongst us to see persons with wry faces and their arms in slings that the more joyful spirits in town are now inces- santly humming this altered version of a popular song:

"Whenever I go out You will hear the people shout Mind your ar-rm." This wholesale vaccination is said to be the cause of the abatement in the epidemic, and therefore it appears to have been a blessing to the town. But whilst admitting all the virtues of the opera- tion, which the medical profession attribute to it, I would draw attention to two dangerous errors which many of the public are inclined to make respecting ,the "Charm." These errors are chiefly prevalent among our poorer brethren. The first is that they consider after inoculation they enjoy an immunity from the disease. The second; which follows upon the first is that they are so confident of this immunity that they neglect the chief pre- ventative of the disease, cleanliness. In an article upon vaccination in the "Surrey Gazette" Mr. C. Lyons, of Warrington ssys : "one conspicuous feature, evincing a serious flaw in the present method, has been brought to light in War- rington, and that is owing to the belief amongst many of the poorer classes in the perfect safeguard of vaccination. Many of them crowd to the houses and bedsides of patients, in all stages of the disease, saying "Oh we have been vaccinated: we are all right I" In one instance as many as 10 women were fonnd in the room of a smallpox patient, When the medical officers' assistants came to remove her. Unfortunately this is only one of the mans distressing instances of ignorance, which is merely on a par with the absurd superstitions of many others of the poor, who refuse to adopt any precaution because they trust in the scrap of musty logic, " If I have to have it, I shall have it." During the past week or two many who have been vaccin- ated were to be seem hanging about the exterior of the hospital, feeling safe from the disease, and sat- isfying a misguided curiosity to see " What's go- ing on." A short time ago the writer saw a child being removed from Scotland-road, and as it was conveyed to the vehicle quite a small crowd of women congregated. They seemed abnormally "full of sympathy, and either carried away by emo- tion, or wishing to test the "charm " of vaccina- tion, they kissed and fondled the child, in spite of instructions to the contrary. This blind attachment to the "charm." existed even when the grim disease was respecting neither vaccinkted nor unvaccinated and persons with their arms inoculated were even , more satisfied than ever to live in filth. Would it not be better if those people were taught to respect vaccination for what it is worth, and place the proper and higher value upon clean- liness and sanitation? But they can never learn this secret until they are assisted to it by the authorities, who are, to a great extent, responsible for their ignorance.. And those authorities, with the recent lesson fresh upon their memories, should set about their task as soon aapossible.
LATEST NEWS

It is officially announced that the Government have resolved not to interefere with the evacuation of Uganda by the British East Africa Company on the 31st March,/ but at once to send a Commissioner of their own, with a sufficient native escort, for the purpose of reportin., on the actual state of affairs there and the beet means of dealing with the country.
CHESHIRE AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY.

The 54th annual report of this society just Issued, contains the following referenced to their recent show at Warrington :—" The General Comss- mittee beg to submit their fifty-fourth annual report of this society, and in doing so beg to tender their cordial thanks to the Mayor of Warrington (Edward Greenall, Esq.) for acting as President for the year ; also for the special prizes given tO Milkers, a new and attractive feature to the show. The society is indebted to the Local Committee for £93 25., given in Prizes and Medals, and also for' their contribution of £250 towards the show yard expenses. Thanks are also due to the Warrington. Shire Horse Society. for holding their annual show on our ground, there by enhancing both the number of entries and the interest in the show generally-- Ihe audited statement of accounts show a balance in the treasurer's hands of £319 16s. 2d., or a decrease since last year of £56 4s. 2d. This reduction may be accounted for by the fact that the admission at the gates is nearly £2OO less than last year, and that the secretary has been unable to collect sundry sums due to the Society. This year's entries (exclusive of those of the Shire Horse ' Society), have proved the most numerous in the Society's- history, the Horse Classes being especially good, both in number and quality." Bd. ; receipts in prizes, from the Warring- ton Local Committee, £93 2s. and the-Warrington Shire, Horse Society, £6O. The expenditure is shown to have been £1,588, Bs. 9d., leaving a balance of £319 16a. 2d. in hand. Among the items of expenses. are ili T. bill-posting, stamps, stationery, a:, £lO9 15s. ; canist and catalogues, £3O 7s. ; judges' and stewards expenses*, refreshments, &c., £5l 38. 11d. ; fitting up show yard, grand stand and tents, gate-keepers, police, Am, £615. ss. 7,1; prizes and medals awarded, including those given by the local Committee, £630 3s. 6d.

ATHLETICS.
FOOTBALL.

Hamlet's description of this globe as a world "flat, stale and unprofitable," was applied often last week by men of sport in Warrington. They applied it to the football wGrld of course. The league match with Sal- ford was caneelled, and so is the one with Widnes booked for next week. Even the junior teams in town were only on " half-time "as it were. There was only one little silver lining in the whole dark cloud, and that was the prospect of seeing Lancashire and Cumberland at Whalley Range.

And this little ray of hope was—in conjunction with some cheap trains—taken advantage of. Quite a large excursion of Warrington people found their way to Whalley Range, chiefly with a view to seeing how Jolley and Boscow would conduct themselves. Most of these Warringtonians congregated together on the field, and a story goes round of how a few of them enjoyed themselves before the game. Amongst the group was a spectator swathed in a huge overcoat which was apparently a family affair—probably constructed for the joint habita- tion of himself and a corpulent brother. But the brother wasn't there. This left a kind of a hungry emptiness about the coat, and when a byestander alluded to the oculiarity the owner didn't like it. He said he didn't and arlded that he reckoned his coat was as good as anybody..?,

The bystandn said : "Taint, not by a jugful. If you suspended a brick round your neck, and accidentally fell in the river, d'ye know what would happen ?" An undertoned growl" 'a fittiat out." "No,nty friend, you would enjoy the falicious privilege of going like some of our unappreciated feline pets—drowned in a bag." It was some time before the spectators could pacify the two men, and things were lively for a time.

The field resembled some huge grass plot with a layer of soft soap on it, and the play throughout was hard and fast. Boscow seemed to be a little nervous at first,which nnite natural. But as the v•ame weot On t 9 Warmed ' 'play 2 tcPttl" f. Cv°;elit-s‘g—Wre.6.sl:77illiiee r4s,t cries of Jo e, ' frOM his friends on the field, Once ho MA a thing which made everyone cheer him. It was near the call of time, three of the Cumberland men broke away with the ball. On they dashed, and then SUCCVS seemed inevitable. Nearer and nearer they got to floscow,who was the only safeguard. Some tricky dribbling commenced, and the Cumberland men would very probably have gained a try if Joe had not quietly stepped between them, put the ball aside with his foot, gathered, and returned it to the Lancastrian domain. Beseow's play throughout gave the greatest satisfaction to all—especially the Lan- cashire Committee.

About half-past nine on Tuesday evening an anxious group of footballers waited for a telegram from the Lancashire Club Committee ,respecting the outcome of their cogitations on Boscow and Jolley's fitness to play against Yorkshire on Saturday. The telegram came, and with it the joyful news that both players had been selected. A great amount of sympathy is felt for " Smack " Bate,who would no doubt have also been chosen as one of the Lancashire 15, had he not received the unfortunate injury last week but one. It is said that if Boscew and Bate could only have played to- gether on Saturday last, the reputation of the Warring- ton wirepullers would have been made.

We refer to Mr. John Connor, son of Mr. Edward Connor, of Sankey-st. He has been invited to play with the Priaston North End team by Mr. Ross, organiser.
