div.head: BAND OF HOPE.
div.p: BAND OF HOPE.

Last evening week the Penketh Wesleyan Band of Hope members held their monthly con ert. Mr. C. E. Parker was in the chair. The concert was a decided improvement on the old style of meetings, the talent being very good. The programme con- sisted of songs, choruses, readings, and recitations, concluding with a laughable dialogue entitled "Paddy's mistake." The ladies and gentlemen tak- ing part in the programme were Messrs. Thompson Travis (Widnes), and J. Lee, stringer, and Minley, Miss Hughes (Widnes), and members of the societ3. The persons in the dialogue were, Misses M. Winner. M. A. Plumpton, and Messrs. J. Lewis, H. Minley, E. Wilkinson, and G. E. Smith. The success of the concert was due to Mr. B. Pardoe, who has had entire charge of the affair.

div.head: MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.
div.p: MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.

On Weirie-s-d;i; evening the first weekly meeting of the above association was held in the Wesleyan Schoolroom, Mr. Hunter in the chair. The essayist was Miss Fanny Garnett and her subject was Lord Tennyson. The essayist treated it as a biographi- cal sketch and gave many interesting incidents in his life. The essay was rendered very interesting by the frequent interspersions of appropriate reci- tat,ons and songs from Tennyson's works. The musical programme consisted of two quartets, "Sweet and Low" and "Crossing the Bar," by Miss Hilda Garnett, Miss Robinson, Mr. T. candy, and Mr. R. E. Garnett. Miss Bessie Dutton, of Moore, read a portion of " Guinivere " and Mrs. Garnett and Mr. T. Gandy also read selections. Mr. R. E. Garnett recited, " The Revenge," and Miss Robinson also sang "Too late." A vote of thanks was passed to the essayist.

div.head: GROCERS' GRIEVANCES.
div.p: GROCERS' GRIEVANCES.
DEPUTATION TO THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD.

The Secretary to the Local Government Board received on Thursday a deputation representing the Federation of Grocers' Associations, who desired an amendment of the Sale of Food and Drugs:Acts, and a more discrimina- ting administration of the provisions of the Margarine Act, both of which Acts, they said, at present operated to the injury of the retail trade. Sir Walter Foster said he hoped that before long there would, even in the rural districts, be set up some authority who would control more effectually the administration of the law. Ile had considerable sympathy with those retail traders who suffered for the sins of others, and agreed that there ought to be some means of protecting the man who innocently sold adulterated articles and of getting at the manufacturer.

Bertie Wood, aged 15, son of a well-known solicitor at Leeds, was shot dead on Wednesday evening, at a Leeds school. While one of the lad's schoolfellows was showing him a revolver the weapon was discharged and a bullet entered Wood's forehead.

AN ELECTION PETITION WITHDRAWN. On 'rhursday, in the High Court of Justice, applica- tion was made to Baron Pollock and Justice Wills on behalf of Sir John Swiuburne, the defeated Gladstomian candidate at the Lichfield election, to withdraw his petition against the return of Major Darwen, the successful Unionist candidate. It was explained that there had been no cellusion between the parties. The withdrawal of the petition was allowed and costs for the respondent granted. ACTION AGAINST LONDON NEWSPAPERS. The Electioc Judges Wills and Pollock, in the Queen's Bench, London, on Thursday, granted a rule nisi re- quiring the publishers of the " Times,"" Standard," and "Morning Post" to show cause why they should not be committed for contempt of court, in publishing a letter from Sir Pryce Jones, respondent in the Montgomery election petition, alleging that artifices cf a discreditable nature were being adopted to trump up the case.

SINGULAR SUICIDE OF A SOLDIER. A retired so' Idler named William Daly committed suicide at Fleetwood on Thursday night by stabbing himself in various parts of the body with a pair of scissors. THE COTTON STRIKE. The North and North-East Lancashire master cotton spinners will not adopt short time to assist the South Lancashire masters. This may have an important bear- ing on the settlement of the dispute. COTTON LADEN TRAIN ON FIRE. _— A fire broke tnit yesterday on a cotton laden train on the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway. The train was stopped between Droylsden and Dbarlesworth stations, and the burning bales were removed and the fire sub- dued. This mishap caused considerable delay in the local traffic. THE UNEMPLOYED IN LONDON. THE PROPOSED MIDNIGHT MARCH. The " Daily Telegraph" states that no torchlight pro- cession at night, such as is alleged to be contemplated by the unemployed, will be allowed to pass through the city. The Scotland-yard authorities state that they have received no intimation that such a demonstration is contemplated. A GOOD " SPREE " SPOILED. Yesterday, at Wigan, Michael Webb, an elderly man was sent to prison for two months, for stealing £IO, the property of Thomas Garrow, of Walton. Prisoner lodged with Garrow, and the meney being missed, information was given to the pollee, who arrested prisoner and found over in his possession. Prisoner remarked that he intended to have a good spree with the money.

TRODSIIIK CONFIRMATION SIIRTICE.—On Wednesday afternoon a confirmation service was conducted in Frodsham Parish Church, by the Bishop of Chester. There was a large congregation. The candidates, numbering 94-47 males and 47 females—came from the parishes of Prod- I sham, Norley, Kingsley, Guilden Sutton, and two from Runcorn. ACCIDENT.—On Tuesday morning a plumber named Henry Potts, employed by Mr. Collinge, of Runcorn, who as engaged completing his contract at the Overton Grammar School, Was, owing to the breakage of a rope, precipitated to the floor from the belfry, sustaining 'severe injuries, including a broken leg. He was con- veyed to the Manchester Infirm ai y. Eremitic Lporrixo.—During the present week the electric light installation which Messrs. T. Rigby and San have been erecting in their flour mills at Frodsham Bridge, has been started to work. It consists of a Crompton dynamo, capable of supplying 150 Edison Swan lamps, of 16-candle power each, and is drives either from the turbine wheel or main engine, as required, , supplying the light direct to the lamps on charging accumulators, as desired. The light is very steady and brilliant. The installation had been carried out by Mr. W. Sillery, electrician, of Wrexham, and is so arranged that all or any portion of the mill and premises can be lighted at once.
